Old King Priam had given his consent and promised her to him, so Othryoneus was fighting on the strength of those promises. Idomeneus aimed a spear and hit him as he came striding on. His bronze breastplate did not protect him, and the spear stuck in his belly; he fell heavily to the ground. Then Idomeneus boasted over him, saying, “Othryoneus, there is no one in the world I will admire more than you, if you actually do what you have promised Priam, son of Dardanus, in return for his daughter. We will make you an offer too—we will give you the loveliest daughter of the son of Atreus, and bring her from Argos for you to marry, if you will help us sack the fine city of Ilium. Come along with me, that we may make a covenant at the ships about the marriage, and we won't be hard on you about courtship gifts.”

With that Idomeneus began dragging him by the foot through the thick of the fight. But Asius came up to protect the body, on foot, in front of his horses, which his charioteer drove so close behind him that he could feel their breath on his shoulder. He was longing to strike down Idomeneus, but before he could, Idomeneus struck him with a spear in the throat under the chin, and the bronze point went clean through it. He fell like an oak, a poplar, or a pine that shipwrights have felled on the mountains with whetted axes for ship's timber—just so he lay stretched out in front of his chariot and horses, grinding his teeth and clutching at the blood-stained dust. His charioteer was struck with panic and did not dare turn his horses around to escape. At that moment Antilochus hit him with a spear in the middle of the body. His bronze breastplate did not protect him, and the spear stuck in his belly. He fell gasping from his chariot, and Antilochus, great Nestor's son, drove the horses from the Trojans to the Achaeans.

Deiphobus then came close up to Idomeneus to avenge Asius and took aim at him with a spear. But Idomeneus was watching and dodged it, for he was covered by the round shield he always carried—a shield of ox-hide and bronze with two arm-rods on the inside. He crouched under its cover, and the spear flew over him, but the shield rang as the spear grazed it. The weapon did not fly in vain from the strong hand of Deiphobus, for it struck Hypsenor, son of Hippasus, shepherd of his people, in the liver under the midriff, and his limbs failed beneath him. Deiphobus boasted over him and cried with a loud voice, “Truly Asius has not fallen unavenged. He will be glad, even as he passes into the house of Hades, strong warden of the gate, that I have sent someone to escort him.”

So he boasted, and the Argives were stung by his words. Noble Antilochus was angrier than anyone, but grief did not make him forget his friend and comrade. He ran to Hypsenor, stood astride him, and covered him with his shield. Then two of his loyal comrades, Mecisteus son of Echius, and Alastor, stooped down and carried him away groaning heavily to the ships. But Idomeneus did not let up in his fury. He kept on striving to shroud some Trojan in the darkness of death, or else to fall himself while warding off the evil day from the Achaeans. Then fell Alcathous, son of noble Aesyetes. He was son-in-law to Anchises, having married Hippodameia, his eldest daughter—the darling of her father and mother, who surpassed all her generation in beauty, accomplishments, and understanding. Therefore the bravest man in all Troy had taken her to wife. Poseidon now laid him low by the hand of Idomeneus, blinding his bright eyes and binding his strong limbs in fetters, so that he could neither step back nor sideways, but stood stock-still like a pillar or a tall tree, when Idomeneus struck him with a spear in the middle of the chest. The coat of mail that had protected his body was now broken, and rang harshly as the spear tore through it. He fell heavily to the ground, and the spear stuck in his heart, which was still beating, and made the butt of the spear quiver until grim Ares put an end to his life. Idomeneus boasted over him and cried with a loud voice, “Deiphobus, since you are in a mood to boast, shall we call it even now that we have killed three men to your one? No, sir—stand and fight me yourself, that you may learn what kind of man I am, descended from Zeus, who has come here. Zeus first fathered Minos, chief ruler in Crete; and Minos in turn fathered a son, noble Deucalion. Deucalion fathered me, to be ruler over many men in Crete, and my ships have now brought me here to be the ruin of yourself, your father, and the Trojans.”

So he spoke, and Deiphobus was of two minds, whether to go back and fetch some other Trojan to help him, or to take up the challenge single-handed. In the end, he thought it best to go fetch Aeneas, whom he found standing at the rear; for Aeneas had long been aggrieved with Priam because, despite his brave deeds, Priam did not give him his rightful share of honor. Deiphobus went up to him and said, “Aeneas, prince among the Trojans, if you hold any ties of kinship dear, help me now to defend the body of your sister's husband. Come with me to rescue Alcathous, who, being your sister's husband, brought you up when you were a child in his house. Now Idomeneus has killed him.”

With these words he stirred Aeneas, and he went in pursuit of Idomeneus, full of great deeds of valor. But Idomeneus was not to be daunted like a mere child. He held his ground like a wild boar at bay in the mountains, who awaits the coming of a great crowd of men in some lonely place—the bristles standing upright on his back, his eyes flashing fire, as he whets his tusks, eager to defend himself against hounds and men—so did famed Idomeneus hold his ground and refuse to budge at the approach of Aeneas. He called aloud to his comrades, looking toward Ascalaphus, Aphareus, Deipyrus, Meriones, and Antilochus, all brave soldiers. “Come here, my friends,” he cried, “and don't leave me alone. I am in great fear of swift Aeneas, who is coming against me—a dreadful dealer of death in battle. And he is in the flower of youth, when a man's strength is greatest. If I were his age, and with my present spirit, either he or I would quickly carry off the prize of victory.”

At this, all of them as one man stood close by him, shield on shoulder. Aeneas, on his side, called to his comrades, looking toward Deiphobus, Paris, and Agenor, who were leaders of the Trojans along with himself. The men followed them as sheep follow the ram when they go down to drink after feeding, and the heart of the shepherd is glad—just so was the heart of Aeneas gladdened when he saw his people following him.

Then they fought furiously in close combat around the body of Alcathous, wielding their long spears. The bronze armor on their bodies rang fearfully as they took aim at one another in the press of the fight, while the two heroes Aeneas and Idomeneus, peers of Ares, outdid everyone in their eagerness to hack at each other with sword and spear. Aeneas aimed first, but Idomeneus was watching and dodged the spear, so that it flew from Aeneas's strong hand in vain and stuck quivering in the ground. Idomeneus meanwhile struck Oenomaus in the middle of the belly and broke the plate of his breastplate; his bowels came gushing out, and he clutched the earth in the palms of his hands as he fell sprawling in the dust. Idomeneus drew the spear out of the body, but he could not strip the rest of the armor because of the rain of darts showered upon him. What's more, his strength was beginning to fail him, so he could no longer charge; he could neither spring forward to recover his own weapon nor swerve aside to avoid one aimed at him. Though he still defended himself in hand-to-hand combat, his heavy feet could not carry him swiftly from the battle. Deiphobus aimed another spear at him as he was retreating slowly from the field—for his bitterness against him was as fierce as ever—but again he missed, and hit Ascalaphus, the son of Ares; the spear went through his shoulder, and he clutched the earth in the palms of his hands as he fell sprawling in the dust.

Grim Ares of the awful voice did not yet know that his son had fallen, for he was sitting on the summits of Olympus beneath golden clouds, by command of Zeus, where the other gods were also sitting, forbidden to take part in the battle. Meanwhile men fought furiously around the body. Deiphobus tore the helmet from Ascalaphus's head, but Meriones sprang on him and struck him on the arm with a spear, so that the visored helmet fell from his hand and came ringing down to the ground. Meriones sprang on him again like a vulture, drew the spear from his shoulder, and fell back under cover of his men. Then Polites, own brother of Deiphobus, passed his arms around his waist and carried him away from the battle, until he reached his horses, which were standing at the rear of the fight with the chariot and their driver. These took him toward the city, groaning and in great pain, with the blood flowing from his arm.

The others kept fighting, and the battle-cry rose to heaven without ceasing. Aeneas sprang on Aphareus, son of Caletor, and struck him with a spear in his throat, which was turned toward him. His head fell to one side, his helmet and shield came down with him, and death, life's enemy, was shed around him. Antilochus saw his chance, flew at Thoon, and wounded him as he was turning. He laid open the vein that runs all the way up the back to the neck; he cut this vein clean through its whole course, and Thoon fell in the dust face-upward, stretching out his hands imploringly to his comrades. Antilochus sprang on him and stripped the armor from his shoulders, glaring around him fearfully as he did so. The Trojans came at him from every side and struck his broad and gleaming shield, but they could not wound his body, for Poseidon stood guard over the son of Nestor, though the darts fell thickly around him. He was never clear of the enemy, but always in the thick of the fight; his spear was never idle; he poised it and aimed in every direction, so eager was he to hit someone from a distance or fight him hand-to-hand.

As he was thus aiming in the crowd, he was seen by Adamas, son of Asius, who rushed at him and struck him with a spear in the middle of his shield. But Poseidon made the point have no effect, for he grudged him the life of Antilochus. Half the spear stuck fast in Antilochus's shield like a charred stake, while the other half lay on the ground. Adamas then sought cover among his men, but Meriones followed after him and hit him with a spear midway between the private parts and the navel—where a wound is particularly painful to wretched mortals. There Meriones pierced him through, and he writhed convulsively around the spear, like a bull that mountain herdsmen have bound with withy ropes and are leading away by force. So he moved convulsively for a little while, but not for long—until Meriones came up and drew the spear out of his body, and his eyes were veiled in darkness.

Helenus then struck Deipyrus with a great Thracian sword, hitting him on the temple in close combat and tearing the helmet from his head; the helmet fell to the ground, and one of the Achaean fighters caught it up as it rolled at his feet. But the eyes of Deipyrus were closed in the darkness of death.

At this Menelaus was grieved, and advanced menacingly toward Helenus, brandishing his spear. But Helenus drew his bow, and the two attacked one another at the same moment—the one with his spear, the other with his bow and arrow. The son of Priam hit the breastplate of Menelaus's corslet, but the arrow glanced off it. As black beans or chickpeas come pattering down on a threshing-floor from the broad winnowing-shovel, blown by shrill winds and shaken by the shovel—just so did the arrow glance off and rebound from the shield of Menelaus. Menelaus in his turn wounded the hand with which Helenus held his bow; the spear went right through his hand and stuck in the bow itself, so that to save his life he retreated under cover of his men, with his hand dragging at his side—for the spear weighed it down until Agenor drew it out and carefully bound the hand in a woolen sling his squire had with him.

Pisander then made straight at Menelaus—his evil destiny luring him to his doom, for he was to fall in fight with you, Menelaus. When the two were close to each other, the spear of the son of Atreus turned aside and he missed his aim. Pisander then struck the shield of brave Menelaus but could not pierce it, for the shield stopped the spear and broke the shaft—yet he was glad and made sure of victory. Then, however, the son of Atreus drew his sword and sprang on him. Pisander seized the bronze battle-axe with its long, polished handle of olive wood that hung at his side under his shield, and the two closed on each other. Pisander struck the peak of Menelaus's crested helmet just under the crest itself, and Menelaus hit Pisander as he was coming at him, on the forehead, right at the rise of his nose. The bones cracked, and his two gore-bedrabbled eyes fell at his feet in the dust. He fell backward to the ground, and Menelaus set his heel on him, stripped him of his armor, and boasted over him, saying, “Even so shall you Trojans leave the ships of the Achaeans—proud and insatiable in battle as you are—nor shall you lack any of the disgrace and shame you have heaped upon me. Cowardly she-wolves that you are, you feared not the anger of dread Zeus, avenger of violated hospitality, who will one day destroy your city. You stole my wedded wife and wickedly carried off much treasure when you were her guest, and now you would hurl fire on our ships and kill our heroes. A day will come when, rage as you may, you shall be stopped. O Father Zeus, you who, they say, stand above all both gods and men in wisdom, from whom all things that befall us come—how can you favor the Trojans so, men so proud and overbearing that they are never tired of fighting? All things pall after a while—sleep, love, sweet song, and stately dance—yet these are things a man would gladly have his fill of, rather than of battle. But of battle the Trojans are insatiable.”
So saying, Menelaus stripped the blood-stained armor from the body of Pisander and handed it over to his men; then he ranged himself again among those in the front of the fight.

Harpalion, son of King Pylaemenes, then sprang on him. He had come to fight at Troy along with his father, but he did not go home again. He struck the middle of Menelaus's shield with his spear but could not pierce it, and to save his life drew back under cover of his men, looking around on every side for fear of being wounded. But Meriones aimed a bronze-tipped arrow at him as he was leaving the field and hit him on the right buttock; the arrow pierced the bone clear through and penetrated the bladder. So he sat down where he was and breathed his last in the arms of his comrades, stretched out like a worm upon the ground, watering the earth with the blood that flowed from his wound. The brave Paphlagonians tended him with all due care; they raised him into his chariot and bore him sadly back to the city of Troy. His father went also with him, weeping bitterly, but there was no ransom that could bring his dead son back to life.

Paris was deeply grieved by the death of Harpalion, who had been his host when he visited the Paphlagonians; so he aimed an arrow to avenge him. Now there was a certain man named Euchenor, son of Polyidus the prophet—a brave man and wealthy, whose home was in Corinth. This Euchenor had set sail for Troy well knowing it would be the death of him, for his good old father Polyidus had often told him he must either stay at home and die of a terrible disease, or go with the Achaeans and perish at the hands of the Trojans. So he chose to avoid the heavy fine the Achaeans would have laid on him, and at the same time to escape the pain and suffering of disease. Paris now struck him on the jaw under his ear, and the life went out of him, and he was shrouded in the darkness of death.

Thus they fought like a flaming fire. But Hector had not yet heard, and did not know, that the Argives were making havoc of his men on the left wing of the battle, where the Achaeans would soon have triumphed over them, so vigorously did Poseidon cheer them on and help them. He therefore held on at the point where he had first forced his way through the gates and the wall, after breaking through the packed ranks of Danaan warriors. It was here that the ships of Ajax and Protesilaus were drawn up by the sea-shore; here the wall was at its lowest, and the fighting of both men and horses raged most fiercely. The Boeotians and the Ionians with their long tunics, the Locrians, the men of Phthia, and the famous force of the Epeans could barely hold Hector back as he rushed on toward the ships, nor could they drive him from them, for he was like a wall of fire. The chosen men of the Athenians were in the van, led by Menestheus, son of Peteos, and with him were Pheidas, Stichius, and stalwart Bias; Meges, son of Phyleus, Amphion, and Dracius commanded the Epeans, while Medon and steady Podarces led the men of Phthia. Medon was bastard son to Oileus and brother of Ajax, but he lived in Phylace away from his own country, for he had killed the brother of his stepmother Eriopis, the wife of Oileus; the other, Podarces, was the son of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus. These two stood at the head of the Phthians and defended the ships together with the Boeotians.

Ajax, son of Oileus, never for a moment left the side of Ajax, son of Telamon; but as two dark oxen strain their utmost at the plow they are drawing across a fallow field, and sweat steams up from the roots of their horns—nothing but the yoke divides them as they break up the ground until they reach the end of the field—so the two Ajaxes stood shoulder to shoulder with one another. Many brave comrades followed the son of Telamon, to relieve him of his shield when he was overcome with sweat and toil, but the Locrians did not follow so close after the son of Oileus, for they could not hold their own in a hand-to-hand fight. They had no bronze helmets with plumes of horsehair, neither shields nor ashen spears, but they had come to Troy armed with bows and with slings of twisted wool, from which they showered missiles to break the Trojan ranks. So the others, with their heavy armor, bore the brunt of the fight against the Trojans and Hector, while the Locrians shot from behind, under cover. The Trojans began to lose heart, for the arrows threw them into confusion.

The Trojans would by now have been driven in sorry plight from the ships and tents back to windy Ilium, had not Polydamas said to Hector, “Hector, there is no persuading you to take advice. Because heaven has endowed you so richly in the arts of war, you think you must therefore excel others in counsel. But you cannot claim pre-eminence in everything. Heaven has made one man an excellent soldier; another a dancer or a singer and player on the lyre; and in yet another Zeus has implanted a wise understanding, from which men reap fruit to the saving of many—and the man himself knows more about it than anyone. So I will say what I think best. The fight has hemmed you in as with a circle of fire, and even now that the Trojans are within the wall, some of them stand aloof in full armor, while others are fighting scattered and outnumbered near the ships. Draw back, then, and call your chieftains around you, so we may decide together whether to fall upon the ships now, in the hope that heaven may grant us victory, or to beat a retreat while we still can. I greatly fear that the Achaeans will pay us yesterday's debt in full, for there is one lingering at their ships who is never weary of battle, and who will not hold aloof much longer.”

So Polydamas spoke, and his words pleased Hector well. He sprang in full armor from his chariot and said, “Polydamas, gather the chieftains here. I will go into the fighting, but I will return at once as soon as I have given them their orders.”

Then he sped on, towering like a snowy mountain, and with a loud cry flew through the ranks of the Trojans and their allies. When they heard his voice, they all hurried to gather around Polydamas, the noble son of Panthous. But Hector kept on among the foremost, looking everywhere for Deiphobus, for prince Helenus, for Adamas son of Asius, and for Asius son of Hyrtacus. Alive and unhurt he could no longer find them, for the last two were lying by the sterns of the Achaean ships, killed by the Argives, and the others had been wounded and stricken down by them. But on the left wing of the dreadful battle he found Paris, husband of lovely Helen, cheering his men and urging them on to fight. Hector went up to him and rebuked him. “Paris,” he said, “evil-hearted Paris, fair to look at but woman-mad and false of tongue, where are Deiphobus and King Helenus? Where are Adamas son of Asius, and Asius son of Hyrtacus? Where too is Othryoneus? Ilium is undone and will now surely fall!”

Paris answered, “Hector, why find fault when there is no one to find fault with? I should hold aloof from battle on any day rather than this one, for my mother did not bear me a coward. From the moment you set our men fighting around the ships, we have been here doing battle with the Danaans. The comrades you ask me about are dead. Deiphobus and King Helenus alone have left the field, both wounded in the hand, but the son of Cronos kept them alive. Now lead on where you would have us go, and we will follow with willing hearts. You shall not find us fail you, as far as our strength holds out, but no man can do more than lies within him, however willing he may be.”

With these words he reassured his brother, and the two went toward the part of the battle where the fighting was thickest, about Cebriones, brave Polydamas, Phalces, Orthaeus, godlike Polyphetes, Palmys, Ascanius, and Morys son of Hippotion—who had come from fertile Ascania the day before to relieve other troops. Then Zeus urged them on to fight. They rushed forth like the blasts of some fierce wind that strike the earth at the front of a thunderstorm—they buffet the salt sea into an uproar; many and mighty are the great waves that come crashing in one after another upon the shore, with their arching heads all crested with foam—so rank behind rank of Trojans in gleaming armor followed their leaders onward. The way was led by Hector, son of Priam, peer of murderous Ares, with his round shield before him—his shield of ox-hides covered with plates of bronze—and his gleaming helmet upon his temples. He kept stepping forward under cover of his shield in every direction, testing the ranks to see if they would give way before him, but he could not daunt the courage of the Achaeans. Ajax was the first to stride out and challenge him. “Sir,” he cried, “come closer! Why do you think to dismay the Argives so vainly? We Achaeans are excellent soldiers, but the scourge of Zeus has fallen heavily upon us. Your heart, I see, is set on destroying our ships, but we too have hands that can keep you at bay—and your own fair town will sooner be taken and sacked by us. The time is near when you will pray to Zeus and all the gods in your flight, that your horses may be swifter than hawks as they raise the dust on the plain and bear you back to your city.”

As he was speaking, a bird flew by on his right, and the host of the Achaeans shouted, taking heart at the omen. But Hector answered, “Ajax, braggart and false of tongue, I wish I were as sure of being son forever to aegis-bearing Zeus, with Queen Hera for my mother, and of being held in equal honor with Athena and Apollo, as I am that this day is big with the destruction of the Achaeans. You shall fall among them if you dare stand against my spear. It shall tear your fair body and bid you glut our hounds and birds of prey with your fat and your flesh, as you fall by the ships of the Achaeans.”

With these words he led the way, and the others followed after with a cry that rent the air, while the host shouted behind them. The Argives, for their part, raised a shout as well; nor did they forget their prowess, but stood firm against the onslaught of the Trojan chieftains. The cry from both hosts rose up to heaven and to the brightness of Zeus's presence.

chapters.title: Book 14
paragraphs: Agamemnon proposes that the Achaeans should sail home, and is rebuked by Odysseus—Hera beguiles Zeus—Hector is wounded.

Nestor was sitting over his wine, but the battle-cry did not escape him, and he said to the son of Asclepius, “What, noble Machaon, is the meaning of all this? The shouts of men fighting by our ships grow louder and louder. Stay here and sit over your wine, while fair Hecamede heats you a bath and washes the clotted blood off you. I will go at once to the lookout and see what is happening.”

As he spoke, he took up the shield of his son Thrasymedes that lay in the tent, all gleaming with bronze—for Thrasymedes had taken his father's shield. He grasped his redoubtable bronze-tipped spear, and as soon as he was outside he saw the disastrous rout of the Achaeans who, now that their wall was thrown down, were fleeing pell-mell before the Trojans. As when there is a heavy swell upon the sea, but the waves are silent—they keep their eyes on the watch for the quarter from which the fierce winds may spring upon them, but they stay where they are and move neither this way nor that, until some particular wind sweeps down from heaven to settle them—so the old man pondered whether to make for the crowd of Danaans or go in search of Agamemnon. In the end he decided it was best to go to the son of Atreus. Meanwhile the armies were fighting and killing one another, and the hard bronze rang on their bodies as they thrust at each other with swords and spears.

The wounded kings, the son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon son of Atreus, fell in with Nestor as they were coming up from their ships—for theirs were drawn up some distance from where the fighting was going on, being on the shore itself since they had been beached first, while the wall had been built behind the hindmost. The stretch of the shore, wide as it was, did not give room for all the ships, and the host was cramped for space; so they had placed the ships in rows one behind the other and had filled the whole opening of the bay between the two points that formed it. The kings, leaning on their spears, were coming out to survey the fight, full of anxiety. When old Nestor met them they were filled with dismay. Then King Agamemnon said to him, “Nestor, son of Neleus, honor to the Achaean name, why have you left the battle to come here? I fear that what dread Hector said will come true, when he boasted among the Trojans that he would not return to Ilium until he had set fire to our ships and killed us. That is what he said, and now it is all coming true. Alas, others of the Achaeans, like Achilles, are so angry with me that they refuse to fight by the sterns of our ships.”

Then Nestor, knight of Gerenia, answered, “It is indeed as you say; it is all coming true this very moment, and even Zeus who thunders from on high cannot prevent it. Fallen is the wall we relied on as an impregnable defense both for ourselves and our fleet. The Trojans are fighting stubbornly and without ceasing at the ships; look where you will, you cannot see from what quarter the rout of the Achaeans is coming. They are being killed in a confused mass and the battle-cry rises to heaven. Let us think, if counsel can do any good, what we had best do. But I do not advise our going into battle ourselves, for a man cannot fight when he is wounded.”

King Agamemnon answered, “Nestor, if the Trojans are indeed fighting at the sterns of our ships, and neither wall nor trench has served us—over which the Danaans toiled so hard, and which they thought would be an impregnable defense both for us and our fleet—then I see it must be the will of Zeus that the Achaeans perish in disgrace here, far from Argos. I knew when Zeus was willing to defend us, and I know now that he is raising the Trojans to equal honor with the gods, while he has bound us hand and foot. So let us all do as I say. Let us bring down the ships that are on the beach and drag them into the water. Let us moor them to their stones a little way out, against nightfall—if by night the Trojans will cease fighting. We may then draw down the rest of the fleet. There is no shame in fleeing ruin, even by night. It is better for a man to flee and be saved than to be caught and killed.”

Odysseus looked fiercely at him and said, “Son of Atreus, what are you talking about? Wretch, you should have commanded some other and baser army, and not been ruler over us to whom Zeus has allotted a life of hard fighting from youth to old age, until every one of us perishes. Is this how you would leave the city of Troy, to win which we have suffered so much hardship? Hold your peace, or some other Achaean may hear you say what no man who knows how to give good counsel, no king over so great a host as the Argives, should ever let fall from his lips. I despise your judgment utterly for what you have just said. Would you have us draw down our ships into the water while the battle rages, and so play further into the hands of the conquering Trojans? It would be ruin. The Achaeans will not keep fighting when they see the ships being drawn into the water; they will cease attacking and keep turning their eyes toward them. Your counsel, sir commander, would be our destruction.”

Agamemnon answered, “Odysseus, your rebuke has stung me to the heart. But I am not ordering the Achaeans to drag their ships to the sea whether they will or no. Someone—old or young—may have better counsel to offer, which I shall be glad to hear.”

Then said Diomedes, “Such a man is at hand; he is not far to seek, if you will listen to me and not resent my speaking, though I am younger than any of you. I am by lineage son of a noble father, Tydeus, who lies buried at Thebes. For Portheus had three noble sons, two of whom, Agrius and Melas, lived in Pleuron and rocky Calydon. The third was the knight Oeneus, my father's father, and he was the most valiant of them all. Oeneus remained in his own country, but my father (as Zeus and the other gods ordained it) migrated to Argos. He married into the family of Adrastus, and his house was one of great abundance, for he had large estates of rich corn-growing land, much orchard ground as well, and many sheep. Moreover, he excelled all the Argives in the use of the spear. You must have heard yourselves whether these things are true or not; therefore, when I speak well, do not despise my words as if I were a coward or of ignoble birth. I say, then, let us go to the fight as we must, wounded though we are. Once there, we may keep out of the battle and beyond the range of the spears, lest we get fresh wounds on top of what we already have, but we can urge on others who have been indulging their tempers and holding aloof from battle until now.”
So he spoke, and they did exactly as he said and set out, King Agamemnon leading the way.

Meanwhile Poseidon had kept no idle watch, and came up to them in the guise of an old man. He took Agamemnon's right hand in his own and said, “Son of Atreus, I suppose Achilles is glad now that he sees the Achaeans routed and slain, for he is utterly without remorse—may he come to a bad end and heaven confound him. As for yourself, the blessed gods are not yet so bitterly angry with you but that the princes and counselors of the Trojans shall again raise the dust on the plain, and you shall see them fleeing from the ships and tents back toward their city.”

With this he raised a mighty battle-cry and sped forward to the plain. The voice that came from his deep chest was as the voice of nine or ten thousand men when they are shouting in the thick of a fight, and it put fresh courage into the hearts of the Achaeans to wage war and do battle without ceasing.

Hera of the golden throne looked down from where she stood on a peak of Olympus, and her heart was gladdened at the sight of him who was at once her brother and brother-in-law, hurrying here and there amid the fighting. Then she turned her eyes to Zeus as he sat on the topmost crests of many-fountained Ida, and she loathed him. She set herself to think how she might deceive him, and in the end she decided it would be best for her to go to Ida and array herself in rich attire, in the hope that Zeus might become enamored of her and wish to embrace her. While he was thus engaged, a sweet and careless sleep might be made to steal over his eyes and senses.

So she went to the room her son Hephaestus had made for her, whose doors he had cunningly fastened by means of a secret key so that no other god could open them. Here she entered and closed the doors behind her. She cleansed all the dirt from her fair body with ambrosia, then anointed herself with olive oil, ambrosial, very soft, and scented specially for herself—if so much as a drop were shaken in the bronze-floored house of Zeus, the scent would pervade the universe of heaven and earth. With this she anointed her delicate skin, then plaited the fair ambrosial locks that flowed in a stream of golden tresses from her immortal head. She put on the wondrous robe Athena had worked for her with consummate art and embroidered with many devices; she fastened it about her bosom with golden clasps, and girdled herself with a girdle that had a hundred tassels. Then she fastened her earrings—three brilliant pendants that glistened most beautifully—through the pierced lobes of her ears, and threw a lovely new veil over her head. She bound her sandals to her feet, and when she had arrayed herself perfectly to her satisfaction, she left her room and called Aphrodite to come aside and speak with her. “My dear child,” she said, “will you do what I am going to ask of you, or will you refuse me because you are angry that I am on the Danaan side, while you are on the Trojan?”
Zeus's daughter Aphrodite answered, “Hera, august queen of goddesses, daughter of mighty Cronos, say what you want, and I will do it for you at once, if I can and if it can be done at all.”

Then Hera told her a lying tale and said, “I want you to endow me with some of those fascinating charms whose spells bring all things mortal and immortal to your feet. I am going to the world's end to visit Oceanus, from whom all we gods proceed, and mother Tethys. They received me into their house, took care of me, and brought me up, having taken me over from Rhea when Zeus imprisoned great Cronos in the depths beneath earth and sea. I must go and see them so I may make peace between them. They have been quarreling and are so angry that they have not slept with one another for a long time. If I can bring them around and restore them to each other's embraces, they will be grateful to me and love me forever after.”
At this, laughter-loving Aphrodite said, “I cannot and must not refuse you, for you sleep in the arms of Zeus, who is our king.”

As she spoke she loosed from her breast the elaborately embroidered girdle into which all her charms had been woven—love, desire, and that sweet flattery that steals the judgment even of the most prudent. She gave the girdle to Hera and said, “Take this girdle in which all my charms reside, and lay it in your bosom. If you wear it, I promise you that your errand, whatever it may be, will not be fruitless.”
When she heard this, Hera smiled, and still smiling she laid the girdle in her bosom.

Aphrodite now went back into the house of Zeus, while Hera darted down from the summits of Olympus. She passed over Pieria and fair Emathia, and went on and on until she came to the snowy ranges of the Thracian horsemen, over whose topmost crests she sped without ever setting foot to ground. When she came to Athos she went on over the waves of the sea until she reached Lemnos, the city of noble Thoas. There she met Sleep, own brother to Death, and caught him by the hand, saying, “Sleep, you who lord it alike over mortals and immortals, if you ever did me a service before, do one for me now, and I shall be grateful to you forever after. Close Zeus's keen eyes for me in slumber while I hold him clasped in my embrace, and I will give you a beautiful golden seat that can never fall to pieces; my clubfooted son Hephaestus shall make it for you, and he shall give it a footstool for you to rest your fair feet upon when you are at table.”

Then Sleep answered, “Hera, great queen of goddesses, daughter of mighty Cronos, I would lull any other of the gods to sleep without hesitation—not even excepting the waters of Oceanus, from whom they all proceed—but I dare not go near Zeus, nor send him to sleep, unless he commands me. I had one lesson already by doing what you asked me, the day when Zeus's mighty son Heracles set sail from Ilium after sacking the city of the Trojans. At your bidding I suffused my sweet self over the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus, and laid him to rest; meanwhile you hatched a plot against Heracles and set the blasts of the angry winds beating upon the sea, until you drove him to the fine city of Cos, far from all his friends. Zeus was furious when he awoke and began hurling the gods about all over the house. He was looking especially for me, and would have flung me down through space into the sea where I should never have been heard of again, had not Night, who cows both men and gods, protected me. I fled to her, and Zeus left off looking for me in spite of his anger, for he did not dare do anything to displease Night. And now you are again asking me to do something I cannot venture on.”

Hera said, “Sleep, why do you take such notions into your head? Do you think Zeus will be as anxious to help the Trojans as he was about his own son? Come—I will marry you to one of the youngest of the Graces, and she shall be your own—Pasithea, whom you have always wanted to marry.”

Sleep was pleased when he heard this, and answered, “Then swear it to me by the dread waters of the river Styx; lay one hand on the bounteous earth and the other on the gleam of the sea, so that all the gods below with Cronos may be our witnesses, and see that you really do give me one of the youngest of the Graces—Pasithea, whom I have always longed to marry.”

Hera did as he asked. She swore, and called on all the gods of the underworld, the Titans, to witness. When she had completed her oath, the two enshrouded themselves in a thick mist and sped lightly forward, leaving Lemnos and Imbros behind them. Soon they reached many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and Lectum where they left the sea to go on by land, and the tops of the forest trees rustled beneath their going. Here Sleep halted, and before Zeus could catch sight of him he climbed a lofty pine tree—the tallest that reared its head toward heaven on all of Ida. He hid himself among the branches and sat there in the guise of the sweet-singing bird that haunts the mountains and is called Chalcis by the gods but Cymindis by men. Hera then went to Gargarus, the topmost peak of Ida, and Zeus, gatherer of clouds, set eyes on her. As soon as he did, he became inflamed with the same passionate desire he had felt when they first enjoyed each other's embraces and slept together without their dear parents knowing. He went up to her and said, “What do you want, that you have come here from Olympus—and that with neither chariot nor horses to convey you?”

Then Hera told him a lying tale and said, “I am going to the world's end to visit Oceanus, from whom all we gods proceed, and mother Tethys. They received me into their house, took care of me, and brought me up. I must go and see them so I may make peace between them. They have been quarreling, and are so angry that they have not slept with one another for a long time. The horses that will take me over land and sea are stationed on the lowermost spurs of many-fountained Ida, and I have come here from Olympus on purpose to consult you. I was afraid you might be angry with me later if I went to the house of Oceanus without letting you know.”

And Zeus said, “Hera, you can choose some other time for paying your visit to Oceanus—for now let us give ourselves up to love and the enjoyment of one another. Never yet have I been so overpowered with passion—not for goddess nor mortal woman—as I am at this moment for you. Not even when I was in love with the wife of Ixion, who bore me Peirithous, peer of gods in counsel; nor with Danaë, the slender-ankled daughter of Acrisius, who bore me the famed hero Perseus. Then there was the daughter of Phoenix, who bore me Minos and Rhadamanthus; Semele, and Alcmena in Thebes, by whom I fathered my lion-hearted son Heracles, while Semele bore Dionysus, the comforter of mankind. There was queen Demeter as well, and lovely Leto, and yourself—but with none of them was I ever so enamored as I am with you now.”

Hera again answered him with a lying tale. “Most dread son of Cronos,” she exclaimed, “what are you talking about? Would you have us enjoy one another here on the top of Mount Ida, where everything can be seen? What if one of the ever-living gods should see us sleeping together, and tell the others? It would be such a scandal that when I rose from your embraces I could never show myself inside your house again. But if you are set on it, there is a room your son Hephaestus made for me, and he gave it good strong doors. If you would have it so, let us go there and lie down.”

And Zeus answered, “Hera, you need not fear that either god or man will see you, for I will enshroud us both in such a dense golden cloud that even the sun, for all his bright piercing beams, shall not see through it.”

With this, the son of Cronos caught his wife in his embrace; whereupon the earth sprouted them a cushion of young grass, with dew-bespangled lotus, crocus, and hyacinth, so soft and thick that it raised them well above the ground. Here they laid themselves down, and overhead they were covered by a fair cloud of gold, from which glittering dewdrops fell.

So the father of all things slept peacefully on the crest of Ida, overcome at once by sleep and love, and he held his wife in his arms. Meanwhile Sleep made off to the ships of the Achaeans to tell earth-encircling Poseidon, lord of the earthquake. When he had found him, he said, “Now, Poseidon, you can help the Danaans with a will, and give them victory, if only for a short time while Zeus is still sleeping. I have sent him into a sweet slumber, and Hera has beguiled him into going to bed with her.”

Sleep then departed and went his way to and fro among mankind, leaving Poseidon more eager than ever to help the Danaans. He darted forward among the first ranks and shouted, “Argives, shall we let Hector, son of Priam, have the triumph of taking our ships and covering himself with glory? This is what he says he will now do, seeing that Achilles is still sulking by his ship. We shall do very well without Achilles if we keep each other in heart and stand by one another. So now let us all do as I say. Let each of us take the best and largest shield we can find, put on our helmets, and sally forth with our longest spears in our hands. I will lead you on, and Hector, son of Priam, rage as he may, will not dare to hold out against us. If any good, staunch soldier has only a small shield, let him hand it over to a lesser man and take a larger one for himself.”

So he spoke, and they did just as he said. The son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon—wounded though they were—set the others in array, and went about everywhere making the exchanges of armor; the most valiant took the best armor, and gave the worse to the worse man. When they had donned their bronze armor, they marched on with Poseidon at their head. In his strong hand he grasped his terrible sword, keen of edge and flashing like lightning; woe to him who meets it in the day of battle—all men quake for fear and keep clear of it.

Hector, on the other side, was drawing up the Trojans. Then Poseidon and Hector waged fierce war on one another—Hector on the Trojan side and Poseidon on the Argive. Mighty was the uproar as the two forces met. The sea came rolling in toward the ships and tents of the Achaeans, but waves do not thunder more loudly on the shore when driven before the blast of Boreas, nor do the flames of a forest fire roar more fiercely when it is well alight on the mountains, nor does the wind bellow with rougher music as it tears through the tops of the oak trees at its hardest, than the terrible shout the Trojans and Achaeans raised as they sprang upon each other.

Hector first aimed his spear at Ajax, who was turned full toward him, and he did not miss. The spear struck him where two bands passed over his chest—the band of his shield and that of his silver-studded sword—and these protected his body. Hector was angry that his spear had been hurled in vain, and withdrew under cover of his men. As he was retreating, Ajax, son of Telamon, struck him with a stone. There were many lying about under the men's feet as they fought—stones brought there to prop up the sides of the ships as they lay on the shore. Ajax caught up one and struck Hector above the rim of his shield, close to his neck. The blow made him spin round like a top and reel in every direction. As an oak falls headlong when uprooted by the lightning-bolt of Father Zeus, and there is a terrible smell of brimstone—no man can help being dismayed if he is standing near it, for a thunderbolt is an awful thing—so Hector fell to earth and bit the dust. His spear fell from his hand, but his shield and helmet were fast about his body, and his bronze armor rang around him.

The sons of the Achaeans came running with a loud cry toward him, hoping to drag him away, and they showered their darts on the Trojans, but none could wound him before he was surrounded and covered by the princes Polydamas, Aeneas, Agenor, Sarpedon captain of the Lycians, and noble Glaucus. Of the others too, not one was unmindful of him, and they held their round shields over him to cover him. His comrades then lifted him off the ground and bore him away from the battle to the place where his horses stood waiting for him at the rear of the fight with their driver and the chariot. These took him toward the city, groaning and in great pain. When they reached the ford of the fair stream of Xanthus, begotten of immortal Zeus, they took him from his chariot and laid him on the ground. They poured water over him, and as they did so he breathed again and opened his eyes. Then, kneeling on his knees, he vomited blood, but soon fell back onto the ground, and his eyes were again closed in darkness, for he was still stunned from the blow.

When the Argives saw Hector leaving the field, they took heart and set upon the Trojans still more furiously. Ajax, swift son of Oileus, began by springing on Satnius, son of Enops, and wounding him with his spear: a fair naiad nymph had borne him to Enops as he herded cattle by the banks of the river Satnioeis. The son of Oileus came up to him and struck him in the flank so that he fell, and a fierce fight between Trojans and Danaans raged around his body. Polydamas, son of Panthous, drew near to avenge him, and wounded Prothoenor, son of Areilycus, on the right shoulder. The terrible spear went right through his shoulder, and he clutched the earth as he fell in the dust. Polydamas boasted loudly over him, saying, “Once again, I see, the spear has not flown in vain from the strong hand of the son of Panthous; an Argive has caught it in his body, and it will serve him as a staff as he goes down into the house of Hades.”

The Argives were maddened by this boast. Ajax, son of Telamon, was angrier than any, for the man had fallen close beside him. So he aimed at Polydamas as he was retreating, but Polydamas saved himself by swerving aside, and the spear struck Archelochus, son of Antenor, for heaven counseled his destruction. It struck him where the head joins the neck, at the top joint of the spine, and severed both the tendons at the back of the head. His head, mouth, and nostrils reached the ground long before his legs and knees could, and Ajax shouted to Polydamas, “Think, Polydamas, and tell me truly whether this man was not as well worth killing as Prothoenor was. He seems rich, and of a rich family—a brother, it may be, or son of the knight Antenor, for he is very like him.”

But he knew well who it was, and the Trojans were deeply angered. Acamas then stood astride his brother's body and wounded Promachus the Boeotian with his spear, for Promachus was trying to drag the brother's body away. Acamas boasted loudly over him, saying, “Argive archers, braggarts that you are, toil and suffering shall not be for us only, but some of you shall fall here as well as ourselves. See how Promachus now sleeps, vanquished by my spear. Payment for my brother's blood has not been long delayed; a man, therefore, may well be thankful if he leaves a kinsman in his house behind him to avenge his fall.”

His taunts infuriated the Argives, and Peneleos was angrier than any of them. He sprang toward Acamas, but Acamas did not stand his ground, and Peneleos killed Ilioneus, son of the rich flock-master Phorbas, whom Hermes had favored and endowed with greater wealth than any other of the Trojans. Ilioneus was his only son, and Peneleos now wounded him in the eye under the eyebrows, tearing the eyeball from its socket. The spear went right through the eye into the nape of the neck, and he fell, stretching out both hands before him. Peneleos then drew his sword and struck him on the neck, so that both head and helmet came tumbling down to the ground with the spear still sticking in the eye. He then held up the head like a poppy-head and showed it to the Trojans, boasting as he did so. “Trojans,” he cried, “bid the father and mother of noble Ilioneus mourn for him in their house, for the wife of Promachus, son of Alegenor, will never be gladdened by the coming of her dear husband—when we Argives return with our ships from Troy.”
As he spoke, fear fell upon them, and every man looked around to see where he might flee for safety.

Tell me now, Muses who dwell on Olympus, who was the first of the Argives to bear away blood-stained spoils after Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, had turned the fortune of war. Ajax, son of Telamon, was first to wound Hyrtius, son of Gyrtius, captain of the staunch Mysians. Antilochus killed Phalces and Mermerus, while Meriones slew Morys and Hippotion. Teucer also killed Prothoon and Periphetes. The son of Atreus then wounded Hyperenor, shepherd of his people, in the flank, and the bronze point made his entrails gush out as it tore through them; at that, his life came hurrying out of him at the place where he had been wounded, and his eyes were closed in darkness. Ajax, son of Oileus, killed more than any other, for there was no man so swift as he to pursue fleeing foes when Zeus had spread panic among them.

chapters.title: Book 15
paragraphs: Zeus wakes, tells Apollo to heal Hector, and the Trojans again become victorious.

But when their flight had taken them past the trench and the set stakes, and many had fallen by the hands of the Danaans, the Trojans halted when they reached their chariots, routed and pale with fear. Zeus now woke on the crests of Ida, where he was lying with golden-throned Hera by his side. Starting to his feet, he saw the Trojans and Achaeans—the one thrown into confusion, the others driving them pell-mell before them with King Poseidon in their midst. He saw Hector lying on the ground with his comrades gathered around him, gasping for breath, wandering in mind and vomiting blood, for it was not the weakest of the Achaeans who had struck him.

The father of gods and men pitied him, and looked fiercely at Hera. “I see, Hera,” he said, “you mischief-making trickster, that your cunning has kept Hector out of the fighting and caused the rout of his host. I am half inclined to thrash you, in which case you will be the first to reap the fruits of your scurvy knavery. Do you not remember how once I had you hanged? I fastened two anvils to your feet and bound your hands in a chain of gold that none could break, and you hung in mid-air among the clouds. All the gods in Olympus were in a fury, but they could not reach you to set you free; when I caught any of them I gripped him and hurled him from the heavenly threshold until he came fainting down to earth. Yet even this did not relieve my mind from the constant anxiety I felt for noble Heracles, whom you and Boreas had spitefully conveyed beyond the seas to Cos after stirring up the tempests; but I rescued him, and notwithstanding all his mighty labors I brought him back again to Argos. I remind you of this, that you may learn to stop being so deceitful, and discover how much you are likely to gain by the embraces with which you have come here to trick me.”

Hera trembled as he spoke, and said, “May heaven above and earth below be my witnesses, with the waters of the river Styx—and this is the most solemn oath a blessed god can take—no, I swear also by your own almighty head and by our marriage bed, things I could never perjure myself over—that Poseidon is not punishing Hector and the Trojans and helping the Achaeans because of anything I did. It is all of his own will, because he was sorry to see the Achaeans hard-pressed at their ships. If I had been advising him, I would have told him to do as you bid him.”

The father of gods and men smiled and answered, “Hera, if you would always support me when we sit in council of the gods, Poseidon, like it or not, would soon come around to our way of thinking. If, then, you are speaking the truth and mean what you say, go among the ranks of the gods and tell Iris and Apollo, lord of the bow, that I want them. Iris, to go to the Achaean host and tell Poseidon to leave off fighting and go home; and Apollo, to send Hector back into battle and give him fresh strength, that he may forget his present sufferings and drive the Achaeans back in confusion until they fall among the ships of Achilles, son of Peleus. Then Achilles will send his comrade Patroclus into battle, and Hector will kill him in front of Ilium after he has slain many warriors, among them my own noble son Sarpedon. Achilles will then kill Hector to avenge Patroclus, and from that time on I will bring it about that the Achaeans shall persistently drive the Trojans back until they fulfill the counsels of Athena and take Ilium. But I will not stay my anger, nor permit any god to help the Danaans, until I have accomplished the desire of the son of Peleus, according to the promise I made by bowing my head on the day Thetis touched my knees and begged me to give him honor.”

Hera heeded his words and went from the heights of Ida to great Olympus. Swift as the thought of a man whose fancy carries him across vast continents, and he says to himself, “Now I will be here, or there,” and he would have all manner of things—just so swiftly did Hera wing her way until she came to high Olympus and went in among the gods who were gathered in the house of Zeus. When they saw her they all came up to her and held out their cups to her in greeting. She let the others be, but took the cup offered her by lovely Themis, who was first to come running up to her. “Hera,” said Themis, “why are you here? And you seem troubled—has your husband, the son of Cronos, been frightening you?”

Hera answered, “Themis, do not ask me about it. You know what a proud and cruel disposition my husband has. Lead the gods to the table, where you and all the immortals can hear the wicked designs he has announced. Many a one, mortal and immortal, will be angered by them, however peaceably he may be feasting now.”

At this Hera sat down, and the gods were troubled throughout the house of Zeus. A smile sat on her lips, but her brow was furrowed with care, and she spoke out in a rage. “Fools that we are,” she cried, “to be thus madly angry with Zeus! We keep wanting to go up to him and stop him by force or persuasion, but he sits aloof and cares for nobody, for he knows he is much stronger than any of the other immortals. So make the best of whatever ills he may choose to send each of you. Ares, I think, has had a taste of them already, for his son Ascalaphus has fallen in battle—the man he loved most dearly of all, and whose father he owns himself to be.”

When he heard this, Ares smote his two sturdy thighs with the flat of his hands and said in anger, “Do not blame me, you gods who dwell in heaven, if I go to the ships of the Achaeans and avenge the death of my son, even though it ends in my being struck by Zeus's lightning and lying in blood and dust among the corpses.”

As he spoke he gave orders to yoke his horses Panic and Rout, while he put on his armor. At this, Zeus would have been roused to still more fierce and implacable enmity against the other immortals, had not Athena, alarmed for the safety of the gods, sprung from her seat and hurried outside. She tore the helmet from his head and the shield from his shoulders, and she took the bronze spear from his strong hand and set it aside. Then she said to Ares, “Madman, you are undone! You have ears that do not hear, or you have lost all judgment and understanding. Have you not heard what Hera has said on coming straight from the presence of Olympian Zeus? Do you wish to go through every kind of suffering before you are brought back sick and sorry to Olympus, having caused infinite mischief to all the rest of us? Zeus would instantly leave the Trojans and Achaeans to themselves; he would come to Olympus to punish us, and he would snatch us up one after another, guilty or not guilty. So lay aside your anger for the death of your son. Better men than he have either been killed already or will fall hereafter, and one cannot protect every man's whole family.”

With these words she took Ares back to his seat. Meanwhile Hera called Apollo outside, along with Iris the messenger of the gods. “Zeus,” she said to them, “desires you to come to him at once on Mount Ida; when you have seen him, you are to do as he then bids you.”

At that Hera left them and resumed her seat inside, while Iris and Apollo made all haste on their way. When they reached many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, they found Zeus seated on topmost Gargarus with a fragrant cloud encircling his head like a diadem. They came into his presence, and he was pleased with them for having obeyed his wife's orders so quickly.

He spoke to Iris first. “Go, swift Iris,” he said, “tell King Poseidon what I now command—and tell him truly. Bid him leave off fighting and either join the company of the gods, or go down into the sea. If he takes no heed and disobeys me, let him consider well whether he is strong enough to hold his own against me if I attack him. I am older and much stronger than he; yet he is not afraid to set himself up as my equal, though all the other gods stand in awe of me.”

Iris, swift as the wind, obeyed him, and like the cold hail or snowflakes that fly from the clouds before the blast of Boreas, she winged her way until she came close to the great shaker of the earth. Then she said, “I have come, dark-haired king who holds the world in his embrace, to bring you a message from Zeus. He bids you leave off fighting and either join the company of the gods, or go down into the sea. If, however, you take no heed and disobey him, he says he will come down here and fight you. He would have you keep out of his reach, for he is older and much stronger than you; and yet you are not afraid to set yourself up as his equal, though all the other gods stand in awe of him.”

Poseidon was very angry and said, “Great heavens! Strong as Zeus may be, he has said more than he can make good if he has threatened violence against me, who am of equal honor with himself. We were three brothers whom Rhea bore to Cronos—Zeus, myself, and Hades, who rules the world below. Heaven and earth were divided into three parts, and each of us was to have an equal share. When we cast lots, it fell to me to have my dwelling in the sea forever; Hades took the darkness of the realms under the earth, while air and sky and clouds were the portion that fell to Zeus. But earth and great Olympus are the common property of all. Therefore I will not walk as Zeus would have me. For all his strength, let him keep to his own third share and be content without threatening to lay hands on me as though I were nobody. Let him keep his bragging talk for his own sons and daughters, who must perforce obey him.”

Swift Iris then answered, “Am I really, Poseidon, to take this defiant, unyielding message to Zeus? Or will you reconsider your answer? Sensible people are open to argument, and you know that the Erinyes always range themselves on the side of the elder.”

Poseidon answered, “Goddess Iris, your words have been well spoken. It is good when a messenger shows so much discretion. Nevertheless, it cuts me to the very heart that anyone should rebuke so angrily another who is his peer, and of like sovereignty with himself. But for now I will give way, in spite of my displeasure. Yet let me tell you—and I mean what I say—if, contrary to the desire of myself, Athena, driver of the spoil, Hera, Hermes, and King Hephaestus, Zeus spares steep Ilium and will not let the Achaeans have the great triumph of sacking it, let him know that he will incur our implacable resentment.”

Poseidon now left the field to go down under the sea, and the Achaeans sorely missed him. Then Zeus said to Apollo, “Go, dear Phoebus, to Hector, for Poseidon, who holds the earth in his embrace, has now gone down under the sea to avoid the full force of my displeasure. Had he not done so, those gods who are below with Cronos would have heard of the fight between us. It is better for both of us that he has curbed his anger and kept out of my reach, for I would have had much trouble with him. Take, then, your tasseled aegis and shake it furiously, to throw the Achaean heroes into panic. Take brave Hector, Far-Darter, into your own care, and rouse him to deeds of daring, until the Achaeans are sent flying back to their ships and to the Hellespont. From that point I will think it over well, how the Achaeans may have a respite from their troubles.”

Apollo obeyed his father's command and left the crests of Ida, flying like a falcon, bane of doves and swiftest of all birds. He found Hector no longer lying on the ground, but sitting up, for he had just come to himself again. He knew those who were about him, and the sweat and hard breathing had left him from the moment the will of aegis-bearing Zeus had revived him. Apollo stood beside him and said, “Hector, son of Priam, why are you so faint, and why are you here away from the others? Has any mishap befallen you?”

Hector in a weak voice answered, “And which, kind sir, of the gods are you, who asks me this? Do you not know that Ajax struck me in the chest with a stone as I was killing his comrades at the ships of the Achaeans, and forced me to leave off fighting? I made sure that this very day I would breathe my last and go down into the house of Hades.”

Then King Apollo said to him, “Take heart; the son of Cronos has sent you a mighty helper from Ida to stand by you and defend you—myself, Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword, who have until now been the guardian not only of yourself but of your city. So now, order your horsemen to drive their chariots against the ships in great numbers. I will go before your horses to smooth the way for them, and will turn the Achaeans in flight.”

As he spoke he infused great strength into the shepherd of his people. And as a horse, stabled and full-fed, breaks loose and gallops gloriously over the plain to the place where he is accustomed to take his bath in the river—he tosses his head, and his mane streams over his shoulders as in all the pride of his strength he flies full speed to the pastures where the mares are feeding—so Hector, when he heard the god's words, urged his horsemen on, and sped forward as fast as his limbs would carry him. As country peasants set their hounds on a horned stag or wild goat—the beast has taken shelter under a rock or in a thicket, and they cannot find it; but suddenly a bearded lion, roused by their shouts, stands in their path, and they lose all further appetite for the chase—so the Achaeans were still charging on in a body, using their swords and double-pointed spears; but when they saw Hector moving among his men, they were afraid, and their hearts sank into their feet.

Then spoke Thoas, son of Andraemon, leader of the Aetolians, a man who could throw a fine spear and was steadfast in close fight, while few could surpass him in debate when opinions were divided. He now, with all sincerity and good will, addressed them thus: “What, in heaven's name, do I see? Is it not Hector come to life again? Everyone made sure he had been killed by Ajax, son of Telamon, but it seems one of the gods has again rescued him. He has killed many of us Danaans already, and I take it will yet do so, for the hand of Zeus must be with him, or he would never dare show himself so masterful in the forefront of the battle. Let us all do as I say: let us order the main body of our forces to fall back on the ships, but let those of us who claim to be the flower of the army stand firm, and see whether we cannot hold Hector back at the point of our spears as soon as he comes near us. I think he will then think better of it before trying to charge into the press of the Danaans.”

So he spoke, and they did as he said. Those who were with Ajax and King Idomeneus, and the followers of Teucer, Meriones, and Meges, peer of Ares, called all their best men about them and sustained the fight against Hector and the Trojans, while the main body fell back on the ships of the Achaeans.

The Trojans pressed forward in a dense body, with Hector striding at their head. Before him went Phoebus Apollo, shrouded in cloud about his shoulders. He bore aloft the terrible aegis with its shaggy fringe, which Hephaestus the smith had given Zeus to strike terror into the hearts of men. With this in his hand he led on the Trojans.

The Argives held together and stood their ground. The battle-cry rose high from either side, and the arrows flew from the bowstrings. Many a spear sped from strong hands and fastened in the bodies of many a valiant warrior, while others fell to earth midway, before they could taste a man's fair flesh and glut themselves with blood. So long as Phoebus Apollo held his aegis quietly and without shaking it, the weapons on either side took effect and the men fell. But when he shook it straight in the face of the Danaans and raised his mighty battle-cry, their hearts fainted within them and they forgot their former prowess. As when two wild beasts spring in the dead of night on a herd of cattle or a large flock of sheep when the herdsman is not there—so were the Danaans struck helpless, for Apollo filled them with panic and gave victory to Hector and the Trojans.

The fight now became more scattered, and men killed one another wherever they could. Hector killed Stichius and Arcesilaus—the one, leader of the Boeotians; the other, friend and comrade of Menestheus. Aeneas killed Medon and Iasus. The first was bastard son of Oileus and brother of Ajax, but he lived in Phylace away from his own country, for he had killed a man, a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis whom Oileus had married. Iasus had become a leader of the Athenians, and was son of Sphelus, the son of Boucolos. Polydamas killed Mecisteus, and Polites killed Echius, in the front of the battle, while Agenor slew Clonius. Paris struck Deiochus from behind in the lower part of the shoulder, as he was fleeing among the foremost, and the point of the spear went clean through him.

While they were stripping these heroes of their armor, the Achaeans were fleeing pell-mell to the trench and the set stakes, and were forced back within their wall. Hector then cried out to the Trojans, “Forward to the ships, and leave the spoils! If I see any man keeping back on the other side of the wall away from the ships, I will have him killed; his kinsmen and kinswomen shall not give him his proper funeral rites, but dogs shall tear him to pieces in front of our city.”

As he spoke he laid his whip across his horses' shoulders and called to the Trojans throughout their ranks. The Trojans shouted with a cry that rent the air, and kept their horses neck and neck with his. Phoebus Apollo went before them, and kicked down the banks of the deep trench into its middle to make a great broad bridge, as wide as the throw of a spear when a man is testing his strength. The Trojan battalions poured over the bridge, and Apollo with his redoubtable aegis led the way. He kicked down the wall of the Achaeans as easily as a child, playing on the seashore, builds a house of sand and then kicks it down again and destroys it. Even so, Apollo, did you shed toil and trouble upon the Argives, filling them with panic and confusion.

So the Achaeans were hemmed in at their ships, calling out to one another and raising their hands with loud cries, every man to heaven. Nestor of Gerenia, tower of strength to the Achaeans, lifted up his hands to the starry firmament and prayed more fervently than any of them. “Father Zeus,” he said, “if ever anyone in wheat-growing Argos burned you fat thighbones of sheep or heifer and prayed to return safely home, and you bowed your head to him in assent, bear it in mind now, and do not allow the Trojans to triumph thus over the Achaeans.”

All-counseling Zeus thundered loudly in answer to the prayer of the aged son of Neleus. When the Trojans heard Zeus thunder, they flung themselves yet more fiercely on the Achaeans. As a wave breaking over the bulwarks of a ship when the sea runs high before a gale—for it is the force of the wind that makes the waves so great—so the Trojans sprang over the wall with a shout and drove their chariots onward. The two sides fought with their double-pointed spears in hand-to-hand encounter—the Trojans from their chariots, and the Achaeans climbing up into their ships and wielding the long pikes that lay on the decks ready for use in a sea-fight, jointed and tipped with bronze.

Now Patroclus, so long as the Achaeans and Trojans were fighting about the wall but were not yet within it and at the ships, remained sitting in the tent of good Eurypylus, entertaining him with conversation and spreading herbs over his wound to ease his pain. When, however, he saw the Trojans swarming through the breach in the wall, while the Achaeans were clamoring and stricken with panic, he cried aloud and struck his two thighs with the flat of his hands. “Eurypylus,” he said in dismay, “I know you want me badly, but I cannot stay with you any longer, for there is hard fighting going on. A servant shall take care of you now, for I must hurry to Achilles and try to persuade him to fight. Who knows but with heaven's help I may convince him? A man does well to listen to the advice of a friend.”

Having spoken, he went on his way. The Achaeans stood firm and resisted the attack of the Trojans; yet though these were fewer in number, they could not drive them back from the ships, neither could the Trojans break the Achaean ranks and make their way in among the tents and ships. As a carpenter's line gives a true edge to a piece of ship's timber, in the hand of some skilled workman whom Athena has instructed in every useful art—so level was the issue of the fight between the two sides, as they fought some around one ship, some around another.

Hector made straight for Ajax, and the two fought fiercely about the same ship. Hector could not force Ajax back and fire the ship, nor could Ajax drive Hector from the spot to which heaven had brought him.

Then Ajax struck Caletor, son of Clytius, in the chest with a spear as he was bringing fire toward the ship. He fell heavily to the ground, and the torch dropped from his hand. When Hector saw his cousin fallen in front of the ship, he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians, “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians good in close fight, do not give up a jot! Rescue the son of Clytius, lest the Achaeans strip him of his armor now that he has fallen.”

He then aimed a spear at Ajax, and missed him, but he hit Lycophron, a follower of Ajax, who came from Cythera but was living with Ajax because he had killed a man among the Cytherans. Hector's spear struck him in the head below the ear, and he fell headlong from the ship's prow to the ground with no life left in him. Ajax shook with rage and said to his brother, “Teucer, my good fellow, our trusty comrade, the son of Mastor, has fallen. He came to live with us from Cythera, and we honored him as much as our own parents. Hector has just killed him. Fetch your deadly arrows at once, and the bow that Phoebus Apollo gave you.”

Teucer heard him and hurried toward him, with his bow and quiver in his hands. At once he showered his arrows on the Trojans, and hit Cleitus, the son of Pisenor, comrade of Polydamas the noble son of Panthous, with the reins in his hands as he was tending to his horses. He was in the middle of the thickest part of the fight, doing good service to Hector and the Trojans, but evil had now come upon him, and none of those willing to do so could avert it, for the arrow struck him on the back of the neck. He fell from his chariot, and his horses shook the empty car as they swerved aside. King Polydamas saw what had happened and was the first to come up to the horses; he gave them over to Astynous, son of Protiaon, and ordered him to watch and keep the horses close at hand. Then he went back and took his place in the front ranks.

Teucer then aimed another arrow at Hector, and there would have been no more fighting at the ships if he had hit him and killed him then and there. But Zeus, who kept watch over Hector, had his eyes on Teucer and robbed him of his triumph by breaking his bowstring just as he was drawing it and about to take aim. At this, the arrow went astray and the bow fell from his hands. Teucer shook with anger and said to his brother, “Alas, see how heaven thwarts us in all we do! It has broken my bowstring and snatched the bow from my hand, though I strung it this very morning that it might serve me for many an arrow.”

Ajax, son of Telamon, answered, “My good fellow, let your bow and arrows be, for Zeus has made them useless to spite the Danaans. Take your spear, lay your shield on your shoulder, and both fight the Trojans yourself and urge others to do so. They may be successful for the moment, but if we fight as we ought, they will find it a hard matter to take the ships.”

Teucer then took his bow and put it aside in his tent. He hung a shield four hides thick about his shoulders, and on his handsome head he set his helmet, well wrought with a crest of horsehair that nodded menacingly above it. He grasped his redoubtable bronze-tipped spear, and at once he was by the side of Ajax.

When Hector saw that Teucer's bow was of no more use to him, he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians, “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians good in close fight, be men, my friends, and show your mettle here at the ships, for I see the weapon of one of their chieftains made useless by the hand of Zeus. It is easy to see when Zeus is helping people and means to help them further, or when he is bringing them down and will do nothing for them. He is now on our side and is going against the Argives. So swarm round the ships and fight. If any of you is struck by spear or sword and loses his life, let him die; he dies with honor who dies fighting for his country, and he will leave his wife and children safe behind him, his house and allotment unplundered, if only the Achaeans can be driven back to their own land—they and their ships.”

With these words he put heart and soul into them all. Ajax on the other side urged his comrades, saying, “Shame on you, Argives! We are now utterly undone unless we can save ourselves by driving the enemy from our ships. Do you think, if Hector takes them, that you will be able to get home by land? Can you not hear him cheering on his whole host to set fire to our fleet, and bidding them remember that they are not at a dance but in battle? Our only course is to fight them with might and main. We had better take our chances—life or death, once for all—than fight long and without issue, hemmed in at our ships by worse men than ourselves.”

With these words he put life and soul into them all. Hector then killed Schedius, son of Perimedes, leader of the Phoceans, and Ajax killed Laodamas, captain of foot soldiers and son of Antenor. Polydamas killed Otus of Cyllene, a comrade of the son of Phyleus and chief of the proud Epeans. When Meges saw this, he sprang at him, but Polydamas crouched down, and he missed him, for Apollo would not let the son of Panthous fall in battle. The spear instead hit Croesmus in the middle of his chest, and he fell heavily to the ground, and Meges stripped him of his armor. At that moment the valiant soldier Dolops, son of Lampus, sprang on him. Lampus was son of Laomedon and noted for his valor, and his son Dolops was versed in all the ways of war. He now struck the middle of the son of Phyleus's shield with his spear, attacking at close quarters, but his good corslet, made of plates of metal, saved him. Phyleus had brought it from Ephyra and the river Selleis, where his host, King Euphetes, had given it to him to wear in battle and protect him. It now served to save the life of his son. Then Meges struck the topmost crest of Dolops's bronze helmet with his spear, and tore away its plume of horsehair, so that all newly dyed with scarlet as it was, it tumbled down into the dust. While Dolops was still fighting and confident of victory, Menelaus came up to help Meges, and got alongside Dolops unperceived. Then he speared him in the shoulder, from behind, and the point, driven so furiously, went through into his chest, whereupon he fell headlong. The two then made for him to strip him of his armor, but Hector called on all his brothers for help, and especially rebuked brave Melanippus, son of Hicetaon, who had once pastured his herds of cattle in Percote before the war broke out; but when the ships of the Danaans came, he went back to Ilium, where he was eminent among the Trojans, and lived near Priam, who treated him as one of his own sons. Hector now rebuked him, saying, “Why, Melanippus, are we so remiss? Do you take no note of the death of your kinsman? Do you not see how they are trying to take Dolops's armor? Follow me; there must be no fighting the Argives from a distance now, but hand-to-hand, until either we kill them or they take the high wall of Ilium and slay her people.”

He led on as he spoke, and the hero Melanippus followed after. Meanwhile Ajax, son of Telamon, was cheering on the Argives. “My friends,” he cried, “be men, and fear dishonor! Acquit yourselves in battle so as to earn respect from one another. Men who respect each other's good opinion are less likely to be killed than those who do not; in flight there is neither gain nor glory.”

Thus did he urge on men who were already bent on driving back the Trojans. They laid his words to heart and hedged the ships as with a wall of bronze, while Zeus urged on the Trojans.
