Menelaus of the loud battle-cry urged Antilochus on. “Antilochus,” he said, “you are young, and there is none of the Achaeans swifter of foot or more valiant than you. See if you cannot spring on some Trojan and kill him.”

He hurried away when he had thus spurred Antilochus, who at once darted out from the front ranks and aimed a spear, after looking carefully around him. The Trojans fell back as he threw, and the dart did not speed from his hand without effect, for it struck Melanippus, the proud son of Hicetaon, in the breast by the nipple as he was coming forward, and his armor rang rattling round him as he fell heavily to the ground. Antilochus sprang on him as a dog springs on a fawn that a hunter has hit as it was breaking from its cover, and killed it. So, Melanippus, did stalwart Antilochus spring upon you to strip you of your armor. But noble Hector marked him and came running at him through the thick of the battle. Antilochus, brave soldier though he was, would not stay to face him, but fled like some savage creature that knows it has done wrong—one that flees, when it has killed a dog or a herdsman, before a body of men can gather to attack it. So the son of Nestor fled, and the Trojans with Hector, with a cry that rent the air, showered their weapons after him; nor did he turn and stay his flight until he had reached his comrades.

The Trojans, fierce as lions, were still rushing on toward the ships in fulfillment of the commands of Zeus, who kept spurring them on to new deeds of daring, while he deadened the courage of the Argives and defeated them by encouraging the Trojans. For he meant to give glory to Hector, son of Priam, and to let him throw fire on the ships, until he had fulfilled the unrighteous prayer Thetis had made. So Zeus bided his time until he should see the glare of a blazing ship. From that hour, he was about to order that the Trojans should be driven back from the ships and give glory to the Achaeans. With this purpose he inspired Hector, son of Priam, who was eager enough already, to assail the ships. His fury was like that of Ares, or like when a fire rages in the glades of some dense forest on the mountains; he foamed at the mouth, his eyes glared under his terrible eyebrows, and his helmet quivered on his temples from the fury with which he fought. Zeus from heaven was with him, and though he was but one against many, gave him victory and glory, for he was doomed to an early death, and already Pallas Athena was hurrying on the hour of his destruction at the hands of the son of Peleus. Now, however, he kept trying to break the ranks of the enemy wherever he could see them thickest and in the finest armor; but do what he might, he could not break through them, for they stood like a tower foursquare, or like some high cliff rising from the gray sea that braves the anger of the gale and of the waves that thunder up against it. He fell upon them like flames of fire from every quarter. As when a wave, raised mountain-high by wind and storm, breaks over a ship and covers it deep in foam—the fierce winds roar against the mast, the hearts of the sailors fail them for fear, and they are saved but by very little from destruction—so were the hearts of the Achaeans fainting within them. Or as a savage lion attacking a herd of cows while they feed by thousands in the low-lying meadows by some wide-watered shore—the herdsman is at his wit's end how to protect his herd and keeps going about, now in the van and now in the rear of his cattle, while the lion springs into the thick of them and fastens on a cow, so that they all tremble for fear—so were the Achaeans utterly panic-stricken by Hector and Father Zeus. Nevertheless, Hector killed only Periphetes of Mycenae. He was son of Copreus, who used to take the orders of King Eurystheus to mighty Heracles; but the son was a far better man than the father in every way—swift of foot, a valiant warrior, and in understanding ranked among the foremost men of Mycenae. He it was who now gave Hector a triumph, for as he was turning back he stumbled against the rim of his shield, which reached his feet and served to keep the javelins off him. He tripped on this and fell face upward, his helmet ringing loudly about his head as he did so. Hector saw him fall and ran up to him; he then thrust a spear into his chest and killed him close to his own comrades. These, for all their sorrow, could not help him, for they themselves were terribly afraid of Hector.

They had now reached the ships, and the prows of those that had been drawn up first were on every side of them, but the Trojans came pouring after them. The Argives were driven back from the first row of ships, but they made a stand by their tents without being broken up and scattered; shame and fear restrained them. They kept shouting incessantly to one another, and Nestor of Gerenia, tower of strength to the Achaeans, was loudest in imploring every man by his parents, and begging him to stand firm.

“Be men, my friends,” he cried, “and respect one another's good opinion. Think, all of you, of your children, your wives, your property, and your parents, whether these be alive or dead. On their behalf, though they are not here, I implore you to stand firm, and not to turn in flight.”

With these words he put heart and soul into them all. Athena lifted the thick veil of darkness from their eyes, and much light fell upon them—alike on the side of the ships and on that where the fighting raged. They could see Hector and all his men, both those in the rear taking no part in the battle and those fighting by the ships.

Ajax could not bring himself to retreat along with the rest, but strode from deck to deck with a great sea-pike in his hands, twelve cubits long and jointed with rings. As a man skilled in feats of horsemanship couples four horses together and comes tearing full speed along the public way from the country into some large town—many, both men and women, marvel as they see him, for he keeps all the while changing his horse, springing from one to another without ever missing his footing while the horses are at a gallop—so Ajax strode from one ship's deck to another, and his voice went up into the heavens. He kept on shouting his orders to the Danaans and urging them to defend their ships and tents; neither did Hector remain within the main body of the Trojan warriors. But as a dun eagle swoops down upon a flock of wildfowl feeding near a river—geese, it may be, or cranes, or long-necked swans—so did Hector make straight for a dark-prowed ship, rushing right at it, for Zeus with his mighty hand impelled him forward and roused his people to follow him.

And now the battle raged furiously again at the ships. You would have thought the men were coming on fresh and unwearied, so fiercely did they fight. And this was the mind in which they were: the Achaeans did not believe they could escape destruction and thought themselves doomed, while there was not a Trojan whose heart did not beat high with the hope of firing the ships and putting the Achaean heroes to the sword.

Thus were the two sides minded. Then Hector seized the stern of the good ship that had brought Protesilaus to Troy, but never bore him back to his native land. Around this ship there raged a close hand-to-hand fight between Danaans and Trojans. They did not fight at a distance with bows and javelins, but with one mind hacked at one another in close combat with their mighty swords and double-pointed spears; they fought moreover with keen battle-axes and with hatchets. Many a good stout blade, hilted and scabbarded with iron, fell from hand or shoulder as they fought, and the earth ran red with blood. Hector, when he had seized the ship, would not loosen his hold but held on to its curved stern and shouted to the Trojans, “Bring fire, and raise the battle-cry, all of you with a single voice! Now has Zeus granted us a day that will repay us for all the rest. This day we shall take the ships that came here against heaven's will and have caused us such infinite suffering through the cowardice of our counselors, who, when I would have done battle at the ships, held me back and forbade the host to follow me. If Zeus did then indeed warp our judgment, he himself now commands me and cheers me on.”

As he spoke, the Trojans sprang yet more fiercely on the Achaeans, and Ajax no longer held his ground, for he was overcome by the darts flung at him, and made sure he was doomed. So he left the raised deck at the stern and stepped back onto the seven-foot bench of the oarsmen. Here he stood on the lookout, and with his spear held back any Trojan he saw bringing fire to the ships. All the while he kept shouting at the top of his voice and urging on the Danaans. “My friends,” he cried, “Danaan heroes, servants of Ares, be men, my friends, and fight with might and main! Can we hope to find helpers hereafter, or a wall to shield us more surely than the one we have? There is no strong city within reach from which we may draw fresh forces to turn the scales in our favor. We are on the plain of the armed Trojans, with the sea behind us, and far from our own country. Our salvation, then, lies in the might of our hands and in hard fighting.”

As he spoke he wielded his spear with still greater fury, and whenever any Trojan made toward the ships with fire at Hector's bidding, he would be on the lookout for him and drive at him with his long spear. Twelve men did he thus kill in hand-to-hand combat before the ships.

chapters.title: Book 16
paragraphs: Fire is now thrown on the ship of Protesilaus—Patroclus fights in the armor of Achilles—He drives the Trojans back, but is in the end killed by Euphorbus and Hector.

So they fought about the ship of Protesilaus. Then Patroclus drew near to Achilles with tears welling from his eyes, like some spring whose crystal stream falls over the ledges of a high cliff. When Achilles saw him weeping he pitied him and said, “Why, Patroclus, do you stand there crying like some silly child that comes running to her mother and begs to be picked up and carried—she catches hold of her mother's dress to hold her back, though she is in a hurry, and looks tearfully up until her mother lifts her—such are the tears, Patroclus, you are now shedding. Have you something to say to the Myrmidons or to myself? Or have you had news from Phthia that only you know? They tell me Menoetius, son of Actor, is still alive, as is Peleus, son of Aeacus, among the Myrmidons—men whose loss we two would bitterly mourn. Or are you grieving about the Argives and the way they are being killed at the ships, through their own high-handed doings? Don't hide anything from me, but tell me, that both of us may know.”

Then, knight Patroclus, with a deep sigh you answered, “Achilles, son of Peleus, foremost champion of the Achaeans, do not be angry—but I weep for the disaster that has now befallen the Argives. All those who have been their champions until now are lying at the ships, wounded by sword or spear. Brave Diomedes, son of Tydeus, has been hit with a spear; famed Odysseus and Agamemnon have taken sword-wounds; Eurypylus has been struck with an arrow in the thigh; skilled physicians are attending to these heroes and healing their wounds. Are you still, Achilles, so inflexible? May it never be my lot to nurse such a passion as you have, to the ruin of your own good name. Who in future story will speak well of you unless you now save the Argives from ruin? You know no pity. The knight Peleus was not your father, nor Thetis your mother; the gray sea bore you and the sheer cliffs begot you, so cruel and remorseless are you. But if you are held back by some oracle, or if your mother Thetis has told you something from the mouth of Zeus, then at least send me, and the Myrmidons with me, if I may bring deliverance to the Danaans. Let me wear your armor; the Trojans may mistake me for you and quit the field, so that the hard-pressed sons of the Achaeans may have breathing time—something they can hardly have while they are fighting. We who are fresh might soon drive tired men back from our ships and tents to their own city.”

He did not know what he was asking, nor that he was begging for his own destruction. Achilles was deeply moved and answered, “What, noble Patroclus, are you saying? I know of no prophecy I am heeding, nor has my mother told me anything from the mouth of Zeus. But I am cut to the heart that one of my own rank should dare to rob me because he is more powerful than I am. After all I have been through, this is more than I can endure. The girl whom the sons of the Achaeans chose for me, whom I won as the fruit of my spear after sacking a city—her, King Agamemnon has taken from me as if I were some common vagrant. Still, let bygones be bygones: no man may keep his anger forever. I said I would not relent until battle and the cry of war reached my own ships; nevertheless, now gird my armor about your shoulders, and lead the Myrmidons to battle, for the dark cloud of Trojans has burst furiously over our fleet; the Argives have been driven back onto the beach, cooped within a narrow space, and the whole people of Troy have taken heart to sally out against them, because they do not see the visor of my helmet gleaming near them. Had they seen it, there would not have been a creek or gully that would not have been filled with their dead as they fled. And so it would have been, if only King Agamemnon had dealt fairly with me. As it is, the Trojans have beset our host. Diomedes, son of Tydeus, no longer wields his spear to defend the Danaans, nor have I heard the voice of the son of Atreus coming from his hated head—whereas that of murderous Hector rings in my ears as he gives orders to the Trojans, who triumph over the Achaeans and fill the whole plain with their battle-cry. But even so, Patroclus, fall upon them and save the fleet, lest the Trojans set it on fire and prevent us from ever returning. Do, however, as I now bid you, that you may win me great honor from all the Danaans, and that they may restore the girl to me again and give me rich gifts into the bargain. When you have driven the Trojans from the ships, come back. Though Hera's thundering husband should put triumph within your reach, do not fight the Trojans further in my absence, or you will rob me of glory that should be mine. And do not, out of lust for battle, go on killing Trojans nor lead the Achaeans on to Ilium, lest one of the ever-living gods from Olympus attack you—for Phoebus Apollo loves them well. Return when you have freed the ships from peril, and let others wage war upon the plain. Would, by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, that not a single man of all the Trojans might be left alive, nor yet of the Argives, but that we two might be alone left to tear aside the mantle that veils the brow of Troy.”

So they spoke. But Ajax could no longer hold his ground for the shower of darts raining on him; the will of Zeus and the javelins of the Trojans were too much for him. The helmet that gleamed about his temples rang with the continual clatter of the missiles pouring onto it and onto the cheek-pieces that protected his face. Moreover, his left shoulder was tired from holding his shield so long—yet for all this, let fly at him as they would, they could not make him give ground. He could hardly draw breath, the sweat rained from every pore, he had not a moment's respite, and on all sides he was beset by danger upon danger.

And now, tell me, O Muses who hold your mansions on Olympus, how fire was thrown upon the ships of the Achaeans. Hector came close up and let drive with his great sword at the ashen spear of Ajax. He cut it clean in two just behind where the point was fastened to the shaft. Ajax, therefore, had now nothing but a headless spear, while the bronze point flew some way off and came ringing down to the ground. Ajax knew the hand of heaven was in this, and was dismayed to see that Zeus had now left him utterly defenseless and willed victory for the Trojans. So he drew back, and the Trojans flung fire upon the ship, which was at once wrapped in flame.

The fire was now flaring about the ship's stern. Achilles struck his two thighs and said to Patroclus, “Up, noble knight, for I see the glare of enemy fire at our fleet! Up, lest they destroy our ships and leave us no way to retreat! Gird on your armor at once while I call our people together.”

As he spoke, Patroclus put on his armor. First he fastened greaves of good make upon his legs, with ankle-clasps of silver; then he donned the cuirass of the son of Aeacus, richly inlaid and studded. He hung his silver-studded sword of bronze about his shoulders, and then his mighty shield. On his handsome head he set his helmet, well-wrought, with a crest of horsehair that nodded menacingly above it. He grasped two redoubtable spears that suited his hands, but he did not take the spear of noble Achilles, so stout and strong, for none of the other Achaeans could wield it, though Achilles could do so easily. This was the ashen spear from Mount Pelion, which Chiron had cut from a mountaintop and given to Peleus, to deal death among heroes. He told Automedon to yoke his horses with all speed, for Automedon was the man he held in honor next after Achilles, and on whose support in battle he could rely most firmly. Automedon then yoked the swift horses Xanthus and Balius, steeds that could fly like the wind: these were the pair that the harpy Podarge had borne to the west wind, as she was grazing in a meadow by the waters of the river Oceanus. In the side traces he set the noble horse Pedasus, whom Achilles had brought away with him when he sacked the city of Eetion, and who—mortal steed though he was—could take his place alongside those that were immortal.

Meanwhile Achilles went about everywhere among the tents, and ordered his Myrmidons to put on their armor. Like fierce ravening wolves feasting on a horned stag they have killed on the mountains, their jaws red with blood—they go in a pack to lap water from a clear spring with their long thin tongues, reeking of blood and slaughter; they know no fear, for hunger drives them—so did the leaders and counselors of the Myrmidons gather around the good squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, and among them stood Achilles himself, cheering on both men and horses.

Fifty ships had noble Achilles brought to Troy, each with a crew of fifty oarsmen. Over them he set five captains whom he could trust, while he was commander over them all. Menesthius of the gleaming corslet, son of the river Spercheius that streams from heaven, was captain of the first company. Fair Polydora, daughter of Peleus, bore him to ever-flowing Spercheius—a woman mated with a god—but he was called son of Borus son of Perieres, with whom his mother was living as his wedded wife, and who gave great wealth to win her. The second company was led by noble Eudorus, son of an unwed woman. Polymele, daughter of Phylas the graceful dancer, bore him; the mighty slayer of Argos was enamored of her as he saw her among the singing women at a dance held in honor of Artemis, swift huntress of the golden arrows; he therefore—Hermes, giver of all good—went with her into an upper chamber and lay with her in secret, whereupon she bore him a noble son, Eudorus, singularly swift of foot and valiant in battle. When Eileithyia, goddess of the pains of childbirth, brought him into the light of day and he saw the face of the sun, mighty Echecles, son of Actor, took the mother to wife and gave great wealth to win her; but her father Phylas raised the child and took care of him, doting on him as fondly as if he were his own son. The third company was led by Pisander, son of Maemalus, the finest spearman among all the Myrmidons next to Achilles's own comrade Patroclus. The old knight Phoenix was captain of the fourth company, and Alcimedon, noble son of Laerceus, of the fifth.

When Achilles had chosen his men and stationed them all with their captains, he charged them sharply: “Myrmidons, remember your threats against the Trojans while you were at the ships during the time of my anger, when you all complained of me. ‘Cruel son of Peleus,’ you would say, ‘your mother must have suckled you on gall, so ruthless are you. You keep us here at the ships against our will; if you are so relentless, it would be better for us to go home over the sea.’ Often you gathered and chided me like this. The hour is now here for those high feats of arms you have so long been pining for—so keep high hearts, each of you, and do battle with the Trojans.”

With these words he put heart and soul into them all, and they closed their companies yet more tightly when they heard the words of their king. As the stones a builder sets in the wall of some high house that is to give shelter from the winds—just so closely were the helmets and bossed shields set against one another. Shield pressed on shield, helm on helm, and man on man; so close were they that the horsehair plumes on the gleaming ridges of their helmets touched each other as they bent their heads.

In front of them all two men put on their armor—Patroclus and Automedon—two men, with but one mind to lead the Myrmidons. Then Achilles went inside his tent and opened the lid of the strong chest which silver-footed Thetis had given him to take on board ship, and which she had filled with shirts, cloaks to keep out the cold, and good thick rugs. In this chest he had a cup of rare workmanship, from which no man but himself might drink, nor would he make offering from it to any other god save Father Zeus. He took the cup from the chest and cleansed it with sulfur; this done, he rinsed it with clean water, and after he had washed his hands he drew wine. Then he stood in the middle of the court and prayed, looking toward heaven, and poured his drink-offering of wine. Zeus, whose joy is in thunder, did not fail to see him. “King Zeus,” he cried, “lord of Dodona, god of the Pelasgi, who dwell afar, who hold wintry Dodona in your sway, where your prophets the Selli dwell around you with their feet unwashed and their couches made on the ground—if you heard me when I prayed to you before, and did me honor while you sent disaster upon the Achaeans, grant me now the fulfillment of yet this further prayer. I shall stay here where my ships lie, but I shall send my comrade into battle at the head of many Myrmidons. Grant, all-seeing Zeus, that victory may go with him; put your courage into his heart, that Hector may learn whether my squire is man enough to fight alone, or whether his might is indomitable only when I myself enter the turmoil of war. Afterward, when he has driven the fight and the cry of battle from the ships, grant that he may return unharmed, with his armor and his comrades, fighters in close combat.”

So he prayed, and all-counseling Zeus heard his prayer. Part of it he did indeed grant him—but not the whole. He granted that Patroclus should thrust back war and battle from the ships, but refused to let him come safely out of the fight.
When he had made his drink-offering and had thus prayed, Achilles went inside his tent and put the cup back in his chest.
Then he came out again, for he still loved to look upon the fierce fight that raged between the Trojans and Achaeans.

Meanwhile the armed band that was about Patroclus marched on until they sprang high in hope upon the Trojans. They came swarming out like wasps whose nests are by the roadside, whom silly children love to tease—so that any passerby may get stung; or again, if a wayfarer going along the road vexes them by accident, every wasp will come flying out in a fury to defend his little ones—with just such rage and courage did the Myrmidons swarm from their ships, and their battle-cry rose heavenward. Patroclus called out to his men at the top of his voice, “Myrmidons, followers of Achilles, son of Peleus, be men, my friends, fight with might and main, that we may win glory for the son of Peleus, who is by far the foremost man at the ships of the Argives—he, and his close-fighting followers. The son of Atreus, King Agamemnon, shall thus learn his folly in showing no respect to the bravest of the Achaeans.”

With these words he put heart and soul into them all, and they fell in a body on the Trojans. The ships rang again with the cry the Achaeans raised, and when the Trojans saw the brave son of Menoetius and his squire all gleaming in their armor, they were daunted and their battalions were thrown into confusion, for they thought the swift son of Peleus must have put aside his anger and been reconciled to Agamemnon. Every man, therefore, looked around to see where he might flee for safety.

Patroclus first aimed a spear into the middle of the press, where men were packed most closely, by the stern of the ship of Protesilaus. He hit Pyraechmes, who had led his Paeonian horsemen from the Amydon and the broad waters of the river Axius. The spear struck him on the right shoulder, and with a groan he fell backward in the dust; at this his men were thrown into confusion, for by killing their leader—the finest soldier among them—Patroclus struck panic into them all. He thus drove them from the ship and quenched the fire that was then blazing, leaving the half-burnt ship to lie where it was. The Trojans were now driven back with a shout that rent the skies, while the Danaans poured after them from their ships, shouting also without ceasing. As when Zeus, gatherer of the thunder-cloud, spreads a dense canopy over the top of some lofty mountain, and all the peaks, the jutting headlands, and forest glades show out in the great light that flashes from the bursting heavens—so when the Danaans had now driven the fire back from their ships, they took breath for a little while. But the fury of the fight was not yet over, for the Trojans were not driven back in utter rout; they still gave battle, and were ousted from their ground only by sheer fighting.

The fight then became more scattered, and the chieftains killed one another where and how they could. The valiant son of Menoetius first drove his spear into the thigh of Areilycus just as he was turning around; the point went clean through and broke the bone, so that he fell forward. Meanwhile Menelaus struck Thoas in the chest, where it was exposed near the rim of his shield, and he fell dead. The son of Phyleus saw Amphiclus about to attack him, and before he could, he took aim at the upper part of his thigh, where the muscles are thickest of all; the spear tore through all the sinews of the leg, and his eyes were closed in darkness. Of the sons of Nestor, one—Antilochus—speared Atymnius, driving the point through his throat, and down he fell. Maris then sprang on Antilochus in hand-to-hand combat to avenge his brother, and stood astride the body, spear in hand; but valiant Thrasymedes was too quick for him, and in a moment had struck him in the shoulder before he could deal his blow. His aim was true, and the spear severed all the muscles at the root of his arm and tore them down to the bone, so he fell heavily to the ground and his eyes were closed in darkness. Thus did these two noble comrades of Sarpedon go down to Erebus, slain by the two sons of Nestor; they were the warrior sons of Amisodorus, who had reared the invincible Chimera, to the ruin of many. Ajax, son of Oileus, sprang on Cleobulus and took him alive as he was entangled in the crush; but he killed him then and there with a sword-blow to the neck. The sword reeked with his blood, while dark death and the strong hand of fate gripped him and closed his eyes.

Peneleos and Lycon now met in close fight, for they had missed each other with their spears. They had both thrown without effect, so they drew their swords. Lycon struck the plumed crest of Peneleos's helmet, but his sword broke at the hilt, while Peneleos smote Lycon on the neck under the ear. The blade sank so deep that the head was held on by nothing but the skin, and there was no life left in him. Meriones gave chase to Acamas on foot and caught him just as he was about to mount his chariot; he drove a spear through his right shoulder so that he fell headlong from the car, and his eyes were closed in darkness. Idomeneus speared Erymas in the mouth; the bronze point went clean through beneath the brain, crashing in among the white bones and smashing them. His teeth were all knocked out, and the blood came gushing in a stream from both his eyes; it also came gurgling up from his mouth and nostrils, and the darkness of death enfolded him.

Thus did these chieftains of the Danaans each kill his man. As ravening wolves seize on kids or lambs, fastening on them when they are alone on the hillsides and have strayed from the main flock through the carelessness of the shepherd—and when the wolves see this they pounce at once, because the strays cannot defend themselves—so the Danaans now fell on the Trojans, who fled with ill-omened cries in their panic and had no more fight in them.

Meanwhile great Ajax kept trying to drive a spear into Hector, but Hector was so skillful that he held his broad shoulders well under cover of his ox-hide shield, ever on the watch for the whirring of the arrows and the heavy thud of the spears. He knew well that the fortunes of the day had changed, but still stood his ground and tried to protect his comrades.

As when a cloud goes up into heaven from Olympus, rising out of a clear sky when Zeus is brewing a gale—with just such panic-stricken rout did the Trojans now flee, and there was no order in their going. Hector's swift horses bore him and his armor out of the fight, and he left the Trojan host penned in by the deep trench against their will. Many a yoke of horses snapped the pole of their chariots in the trench and left their masters' cars behind them. Patroclus gave chase, calling impetuously on the Danaans and full of fury against the Trojans, who, no longer in a body, filled all the ways with their cries of panic and rout. The air was darkened by the clouds of dust they raised, and the horses strained every nerve in their flight from the tents and ships toward the city.

Patroclus kept heading his horses wherever he saw most men fleeing in confusion, cheering his own men on all the while. Chariots were being smashed in every direction, and many a man came tumbling down from his own car to fall beneath the wheels of Patroclus's, whose immortal steeds, given by the gods to Peleus, sprang over the trench at a bound as they sped onward. He was intent on trying to reach Hector, for he had set his heart on spearing him, but Hector's horses were now hurrying him away. As the whole dark earth bows before some tempest on an autumn day, when Zeus rains his hardest to punish men for giving crooked judgment in their courts and driving justice out without heed to the decrees of heaven—all the rivers run full and the torrents tear many a new channel as they roar headlong from the mountains to the dark sea, and it goes ill with the works of men—just such was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses in their flight.

Patroclus now cut off the battalions nearest him and drove them back toward the ships. They were doing their best to reach the city, but he would not let them, and bore down on them between the river and the ships and wall. Many a fallen comrade did he then avenge. First he hit Pronous with a spear in the chest, where it was exposed near the rim of his shield, and he fell heavily to the ground. Next he sprang on Thestor, son of Enops, who was sitting all huddled up in his chariot, for he had lost his head and the reins had been torn from his hands. Patroclus went up to him and drove a spear into his right jaw; he thus hooked him by the teeth, and the spear pulled him over the rim of his car, as one who sits at the end of some jutting rock and draws a strong fish out of the sea with hook and line—just so, with his spear, did Patroclus pull Thestor all gaping from his chariot. He then threw him down on his face, and he died as he fell. Then, as Erylaus was coming to attack him, he struck him full on the head with a stone, and his brains were all battered inside his helmet, so he fell headlong to the ground and the pangs of death took hold of him. Then he laid low, one after another, Erymas, Amphoterus, Epaltes, Tlepolemus, Echius son of Damastor, Pyris, Ipheus, Euippus, and Polymelus, son of Argeas.

Now when Sarpedon saw his comrades—men who wore ungirdled tunics—being overcome by Patroclus, son of Menoetius, he rebuked the Lycians, saying, “Shame on you! Where are you fleeing? Show your mettle! I myself will meet this man in fight and learn who it is that is so masterful. He has done us much harm, and has stretched many a brave man on the ground.”

He sprang from his chariot as he spoke, and Patroclus, when he saw this, leaped to the ground as well. The two then rushed at one another with loud cries, like eagle-beaked, crook-taloned vultures that scream and tear at one another in some high mountain fastness.

The son of scheming Cronos looked down upon them in pity and said to Hera, who was his wife and sister, “Alas, that it should be the lot of Sarpedon, whom I love so dearly, to perish by the hand of Patroclus. I am of two minds—whether to catch him up out of the fight and set him down safe and sound in the fertile land of Lycia, or to let him now fall by the hand of the son of Menoetius.”

Hera answered, “Most dread son of Cronos, what is this you are saying? Would you snatch a mortal man, whose doom has long been fated, from the jaws of death? Do as you will, but we shall not all be of your mind. I say further, and lay my saying to your heart: if you send Sarpedon safely to his own home, some other of the gods will also want to escort his son out of battle, for there are many sons of gods fighting around the city of Troy, and you will make every one of them jealous. If, however, you are fond of him and pity him, let him indeed fall by the hand of Patroclus; but as soon as the life is gone out of him, send Death and sweet Sleep to bear him off the field and take him to the broad lands of Lycia, where his brothers and his kinsmen will bury him with mound and pillar, in due honor to the dead.”
The father of gods and men assented, but he shed a rain of blood upon the earth in honor of his son, whom Patroclus was about to kill on the rich plain of Troy, far from his home.

When they had come close to one another, Patroclus struck Thrasydemus, the brave squire of Sarpedon, in the lower part of the belly, and killed him. Sarpedon then aimed a spear at Patroclus and missed him, but he struck the horse Pedasus in the right shoulder, and it screamed aloud as it lay, groaning in the dust until the life went out of it. The other two horses began to plunge; the pole of the chariot cracked, and they got entangled in the reins through the fall of the horse that was yoked alongside them; but Automedon knew what to do. Without losing a moment, he drew the keen blade that hung at his sturdy thigh and cut the third horse free; whereupon the other two righted themselves, and pulling hard at the reins, went together back into battle.

Sarpedon now took a second aim at Patroclus, and again missed him; the point of the spear passed over his left shoulder without hitting him. Patroclus then aimed in his turn, and the spear did not speed from his hand in vain, for he hit Sarpedon just where the midriff surrounds the ever-beating heart. He fell like some oak, silver poplar, or tall pine to which woodcutters have laid their axes upon the mountains to make timber for shipbuilding—so did he lie stretched full-length in front of his chariot and horses, moaning and clutching at the blood-stained dust. As when a lion springs with a bound upon a herd of cattle and fastens on a great black bull that dies bellowing in its clutches—so did the leader of the Lycian warriors struggle in death as he fell by the hand of Patroclus. He called on his trusty comrade and said, “Glaucus, my brother, hero among heroes, put forth all your strength, fight with might and main, now if ever acquit yourself like a valiant soldier. First go around among the Lycian captains and bid them fight for Sarpedon; then do battle yourself to save my armor from being taken. My name will haunt you, now and forever, if the Achaeans rob me of my armor now that I have fallen at their ships. Do your very utmost, and call all my people together.”

Death closed his eyes as he spoke. Patroclus planted his heel on his chest and drew the spear from his body, whereupon his senses came out along with it, and he drew out both spear-point and Sarpedon's soul at the same time. Close by, the Myrmidons held his snorting horses, wild with panic at finding themselves deserted by their lords.

Glaucus was overcome with grief when he heard what Sarpedon said, for he could not help him. He had to support his arm with his other hand, being in great pain from the wound Teucer's arrow had given him when Teucer was defending the wall as he, Glaucus, was assaulting it. Therefore he prayed to far-darting Apollo, saying, “Hear me, O king from your seat—be it in the rich land of Lycia or in Troy, for in all places you can hear the prayer of one in distress, as I am now. I have a grievous wound; my hand is aching with pain, there is no stanching the blood, and my whole arm drags because of my injury, so that I cannot grasp my sword nor go among my foes and fight them—though our prince, Zeus's son Sarpedon, is slain. Zeus did not defend his own son. So do you, O king, heal me of my wound, ease my pain, and grant me strength, both to cheer on the Lycians and to fight alongside them round the body of him who has fallen.”

So he prayed, and Apollo heard his prayer. He eased his pain, stanched the black blood from the wound, and gave him new strength. Glaucus perceived this and was thankful that the mighty god had answered his prayer. At once he went among the Lycian captains and bade them come to fight around the body of Sarpedon. From these he strode on among the Trojans to Polydamas, son of Panthous, and Agenor; then he went in search of Aeneas and Hector, and when he had found them he said, “Hector, you have utterly forgotten your allies, who languish here for your sake far from friends and home, while you do nothing to support them. Sarpedon, leader of the Lycian warriors, has fallen—he who was at once the right and might of Lycia. Ares has laid him low by the spear of Patroclus. Stand by him, my friends, and do not let the Myrmidons strip him of his armor, nor treat his body with contempt in revenge for all the Danaans we have speared at the ships.”

As he spoke, the Trojans were plunged into extreme and ungovernable grief; for Sarpedon, alien though he was, had been one of the main stays of their city, both as having many people with him and himself the foremost among them all. Led by Hector, who was infuriated by the fall of Sarpedon, they made instantly for the Danaans with all their might, while the undaunted spirit of Patroclus, son of Menoetius, cheered on the Achaeans. First he spoke to the two Ajaxes, men who needed no prompting. “Ajaxes,” he said, “now let it please you to show yourselves the men you have always been, or even better—Sarpedon has fallen, he who was first to leap over the wall of the Achaeans. Let us take the body and outrage it; let us strip the armor from his shoulders, and kill his comrades if they try to rescue his body.”

He spoke to men who of themselves were fully eager. Both sides—the Trojans and Lycians on the one hand, the Myrmidons and Achaeans on the other—strengthened their battalions and fought desperately around the body of Sarpedon, shouting fiercely all the while. Mighty was the din of their armor as they came together, and Zeus shed a thick darkness over the fight, to increase the toil of the battle over the body of his son.

At first the Trojans made some headway against the Achaeans, for one of the best men among the Myrmidons was killed—Epeigeus, son of noble Agacles, who had once been king in the good city of Budeum; but presently, having killed a valiant kinsman of his own, he had taken refuge with Peleus and Thetis, who sent him to Ilium, the land of noble steeds, to fight the Trojans under Achilles. Hector now struck him on the head with a stone just as he had caught hold of the body, and his brains inside his helmet were all battered in, so that he fell face-foremost upon the body of Sarpedon, and there died. Patroclus was enraged by the death of his comrade, and sped through the front ranks as swiftly as a hawk that swoops on a flock of daws or starlings. Just so swiftly, noble knight Patroclus, did you make straight for the Lycians and Trojans to avenge your comrade. At once he struck Sthenelaus, son of Ithaemenes, on the neck with a stone, breaking the tendons that join it to the head and spine. At this, Hector and the front rank of his men gave ground. As far as a man can throw a javelin when competing for a prize, or even in battle—so far did the Trojans now retreat before the Achaeans. Glaucus, captain of the Lycians, was the first to rally them by killing Bathycles, son of Chalcon, who lived in Hellas and was the richest man among the Myrmidons. Glaucus turned round suddenly, just as Bathycles, who was pursuing him, was about to lay hold of him, and drove his spear right into the middle of his chest, whereupon he fell heavily to the ground. The fall of so good a man filled the Achaeans with dismay, while the Trojans were exultant and came up in a body around the corpse. Nevertheless, the Achaeans, mindful of their prowess, bore straight down on them.

Meriones then killed a helmeted warrior of the Trojans, Laogonus, son of Onetor, who was priest of Zeus of Mount Ida and was honored by the people as a god. Meriones struck him under the jaw and ear, so that life went out of him and the darkness of death laid hold of him. Aeneas then aimed a spear at Meriones, hoping to hit him under the shield as he was advancing, but Meriones saw it coming and stooped forward to avoid it; the spear flew past him and the point stuck in the ground, while the butt-end went on quivering until Ares robbed it of its force. The spear, therefore, sped from Aeneas's hand in vain and fell quivering to the ground. Aeneas was angry and said, “Meriones, you are a good dancer, but if I had hit you, my spear would soon have made an end of you.”

Meriones answered, “Aeneas, for all your bravery, you will not be able to make an end of every one who comes against you. You are only a mortal like myself, and if I were to hit you in the middle of your shield with my spear, however strong and self-confident you may be, I would soon vanquish you, and you would yield your life to Hades of the noble steeds.”

At this the son of Menoetius rebuked him, saying, “Meriones, hero though you are, you should not talk like this. Taunting speeches, my good friend, will not make the Trojans draw away from the dead body; some of them must go under the ground first. Blows are for battle, words for council. So fight, and say nothing.”

He led the way as he spoke, and the hero went forward with him. As the sound of woodcutters in some forest glade on the mountains—and the thud of their axes is heard afar—so now rose a din from the earth, the clash of bronze armor and of good ox-hide shields as men struck each other with their swords and double-pointed spears. A man would have needed good eyesight now to know Sarpedon, so covered was he from head to foot with spears and blood and dust. Men swarmed about the body as flies that buzz round the full milk-pails in spring when they are brimming with milk—so did they gather around Sarpedon; nor did Zeus turn his keen eyes away from the fight for one moment, but kept looking at it all the while, settling how best to kill Patroclus, and considering whether Hector should be allowed to end him now in the fight round the body of Sarpedon, and strip him of his armor, or whether he should let him give yet further trouble to the Trojans. In the end, he decided it was best that the brave squire of Achilles should drive Hector and the Trojans back toward the city and take the lives of many. First, therefore, he made Hector turn fainthearted, whereupon he mounted his chariot and fled, bidding the other Trojans flee also, for he saw that the scales of Zeus had turned against him. Nor would the brave Lycians stand firm; they were dismayed when they saw their king lying struck to the heart amid a heap of corpses—for when the son of Cronos made the fight grow hot, many had fallen above him. The Achaeans, therefore, stripped the gleaming armor from his shoulders, and the brave son of Menoetius gave it to his men to take to the ships. Then Zeus, lord of the storm-cloud, said to Apollo, “Dear Phoebus, go, I pray you, and take Sarpedon out of range of the weapons. Cleanse the black blood from off him, and then bear him a long way off, where you may wash him in the river, anoint him with ambrosia, and clothe him in immortal raiment. This done, commit him to the arms of the two swift messengers, Death and Sleep, who will carry him straight to the rich land of Lycia, where his brothers and kinsmen will bury him, and will raise both mound and pillar to his memory, in due honor to the dead.”

So he spoke. Apollo obeyed his father's command, and came down from the heights of Ida into the thick of the fight. He at once took Sarpedon out of range of the weapons, and then bore him a long way off, where he washed him in the river, anointed him with ambrosia, and clothed him in immortal raiment. This done, he committed him to the arms of the two swift messengers, Death and Sleep, who presently set him down in the rich land of Lycia.

Meanwhile Patroclus, with many a shout to his horses and to Automedon, pursued the Trojans and Lycians in the pride and foolishness of his heart. Had he but obeyed the orders of the son of Peleus, he would have escaped death and been unharmed. But the counsels of Zeus pass man's understanding; he will put even a brave man to flight and snatch victory from his grasp, or again he will set him on to fight—as he now did when he put a high spirit into the heart of Patroclus.

Who then first, and who last, was slain by you, Patroclus, when the gods had called you to meet your doom? First Adrestus, Autonous, Echeclus, Perimus the son of Megas, Epistor and Melanippus; after these he killed Elasus, Mulius, and Pylartes. These he slew, but the rest saved themselves by flight.

The sons of the Achaeans would now have taken Troy by the hands of Patroclus, for his spear flew in all directions, had not Phoebus Apollo taken his stand upon the wall to defeat his purpose and to aid the Trojans. Three times did Patroclus charge an angle of the high wall, and three times did Apollo beat him back, striking his shield with his own immortal hands. When Patroclus was coming on like a god for a fourth time, Apollo shouted at him with an awful voice and said, “Draw back, noble Patroclus. It is not your lot to sack the city of the Trojan chieftains, nor yet will it be that of Achilles, who is a far better man than you.” On hearing this, Patroclus withdrew to some distance and avoided the anger of Apollo.

Meanwhile Hector was waiting with his horses inside the Scaean gates, in doubt whether to drive out again and go on fighting, or to call the army inside the gates. As he was thus hesitating, Phoebus Apollo drew near to him in the likeness of a young, lusty warrior—Asius, who was Hector's uncle, own brother of Hecuba and son of Dymas who lived in Phrygia by the waters of the river Sangarius. In his likeness, Zeus's son Apollo now spoke to Hector, saying, “Hector, why have you stopped fighting? It is unworthy of you. If I were as much better a man than you, as I am worse, you would soon rue your slackness. Drive straight at Patroclus, and see if Apollo may grant you a triumph over him, and you may yet master him.”

With this the god went back into the uproar, and Hector told Cebriones to drive again into the fight. Apollo passed in among them and struck panic into the Argives, while giving triumph to Hector and the Trojans. Hector let the other Danaans alone and killed no man, but drove straight at Patroclus. Patroclus then sprang from his chariot to the ground, with a spear in his left hand and, in his right, a jagged stone as large as his hand could hold. He stood still and threw it; nor did it go far without hitting someone. The cast was not in vain, for the stone struck Cebriones, Hector's charioteer, a bastard son of Priam, as he held the reins in his hands. The stone hit him on the forehead and drove his brows into his head, for the bone was smashed, and his eyes fell to the ground at his feet. He dropped dead from his chariot as though he were diving, and there was no life left in him. Over him you then boasted, knight Patroclus, saying, “Bless my heart, how active he is, and how well he dives! If we had been at sea, this fellow would have dived from the ship's side and brought up as many oysters as the whole crew could stomach, even in rough water, for he has dived beautifully off his chariot onto the ground. It seems, then, that there are divers among the Trojans too.”

As he spoke, he flung himself on Cebriones with the spring, as it were, of a lion that while attacking a stockyard is himself struck in the chest, and his own courage proves his ruin—so furiously, Patroclus, did you then spring upon Cebriones. Hector sprang also from his chariot to the ground. The pair then fought over the body of Cebriones. As two lions fight fiercely on some high mountain over the body of a stag they have killed, so did these two mighty warriors, Patroclus, son of Menoetius, and brave Hector, hack and hew at one another over the corpse of Cebriones. Hector would not let go once he had got him by the head, while Patroclus kept fast hold of his feet, and a fierce fight raged between the other Danaans and Trojans. As the east and south wind buffet one another when they beat upon some dense forest on the mountains—there is beech, and ash, and spreading cornel; the tops of the trees roar as they beat against one another, and one can hear the boughs cracking and breaking—just so did the Trojans and Achaeans spring upon each other and lay about, and neither side would give way. Many a pointed spear fell to the ground, and many a winged arrow sped from its bowstring around the body of Cebriones; many a great stone, moreover, beat on many a shield as they fought around him. But there he lay in the whirling clouds of dust, all huge and hugely, heedless now of his driving.

So long as the sun was still high in mid-heaven, the weapons of either side were alike deadly, and men fell; but when the sun went down toward the time when men unyoke their oxen, the Achaeans proved to be, beyond all forecast, the stronger, so that they drew Cebriones out of range of the darts and tumult of the Trojans, and stripped the armor from his shoulders. Then Patroclus sprang like Ares with fierce intent and a terrific shout upon the Trojans, and three times he killed nine men. But as he was coming on like a god for the fourth time, then, Patroclus, was the hour of your end approaching, for Phoebus fought you in deadly earnest. Patroclus did not see him as he moved about in the crush, for he was enshrouded in thick darkness; and the god struck him from behind on his back and broad shoulders with the flat of his hand, so that his eyes turned dizzy. Phoebus Apollo beat the helmet from his head, and it rolled rattling off under the horses' feet, where its horsehair plumes were all begrimed with dust and blood. Never indeed had that helmet fared so before, for it had served to protect the head and comely forehead of the godlike hero Achilles. Now, however, Zeus delivered it over to be worn by Hector. Yet the end of Hector also was near. The bronze-tipped spear, so great and so strong, was broken in the hand of Patroclus, while his shield that covered him from head to foot fell to the ground, as did also the band that held it, and Apollo undid the fastenings of his corslet.

At this his mind became clouded; his limbs failed him, and he stood as one dazed. Then Euphorbus, son of Panthous, a Dardanian, the best spearman of his time and also the finest horseman and swiftest runner, came behind him and struck him in the back with a spear, midway between the shoulders. This man, as soon as ever he had come up with his chariot, had dismounted twenty men, so proficient was he in all the arts of war—he it was, knight Patroclus, who first drove a weapon into you, but he did not quite overpower you. Euphorbus then ran back into the crowd, after drawing his ashen spear out of the wound; he would not stand firm and wait for Patroclus, unarmed though he now was, to attack him. But Patroclus, unnerved alike by the blow the god had given him and by the spear-wound, drew back under cover of his men in fear for his life. Hector at this, seeing him wounded and giving ground, forced his way through the ranks, and when close up with him struck him in the lower part of the belly with a spear, driving the bronze point right through him, so that he fell heavily to the ground, to the great grief of the Achaeans. As when a lion has fought some fierce wild boar and bested him—the two fight furiously upon the mountains over some little fountain at which they would both drink, and the lion has beaten the boar until he can hardly breathe—so did Hector, son of Priam, take the life of the brave son of Menoetius, who had killed so many, striking him from close at hand and boasting over him the while. “Patroclus,” he said, “you thought you would sack our city, rob our Trojan women of their freedom, and carry them off in your ships to your own country. Fool! Hector and his swift horses were ever straining their utmost to defend them. I am foremost of all the Trojan warriors to keep the day of bondage from them; as for you, vultures shall devour you here. Poor wretch, Achilles with all his bravery availed you nothing—and yet I think when you left him he charged you strictly, saying, ‘Do not come back to the ships, knight Patroclus, until you have torn the blood-stained shirt of murderous Hector about his body.’ Thus, I think, did he charge you, and your fool's heart answered him ‘yes.’”

Then, as the life ebbed out of you, you answered, knight Patroclus: “Hector, boast as you will, for Zeus the son of Cronos and Apollo have granted you victory; it is they who have vanquished me so easily, they who have stripped the armor from my shoulders. Had twenty such men as you attacked me, all of them would have fallen before my spear. Fate and the son of Leto have overpowered me, and among mortal men Euphorbus; you are yourself only third in the killing of me. I say further, and lay my saying to your heart: you too shall live but for a little season. Death and the day of your doom are close upon you, and they will lay you low by the hand of Achilles, son of Aeacus.”

When he had thus spoken, his eyes were closed in death; his soul left his body and flitted down to the house of Hades, mourning its sad fate and bidding farewell to the youth and vigor of its manhood. Dead though he was, Hector still spoke to him, saying, “Patroclus, why should you foretell my doom? Who knows but Achilles, son of lovely Thetis, may be smitten by my spear and die before me?”

As he spoke he drew the bronze spear from the wound, planting his foot upon the body, which he thrust off and let lie on its back. He then went with spear in hand after Automedon, squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, for he longed to bring him down. But the immortal steeds which the gods had given as a rich gift to Peleus bore him swiftly from the field.

chapters.title: Book 17
paragraphs: The fight around the body of Patroclus.

Brave Menelaus, son of Atreus, now learned that Patroclus had fallen, and made his way through the front ranks clad in full armor to stand astride him. As a cow stands lowing over her first calf, so did yellow-haired Menelaus stand astride Patroclus. He held his round shield and his spear in front of him, resolute to kill any who dared face him. But the son of Panthous had also noted the body, and came up to Menelaus, saying, “Menelaus, son of Atreus, draw back, leave the body, and let the blood-stained spoils be. I was first of the Trojans and their brave allies to drive my spear into Patroclus; let me therefore have my full glory among them, or I will take aim and kill you.”

To this Menelaus answered in great anger, “By Father Zeus, boasting is an ill thing. The leopard is not more bold, nor the lion, nor the savage wild boar—fiercest and most fearless of all creatures—than are the proud sons of Panthous. Yet Hyperenor did not see out the days of his youth when he made light of me and stood against me, deeming me the meanest soldier among the Danaans. His own feet never bore him back to gladden his wife and parents. Even so shall I make an end of you too, if you stand against me. Get yourself back into the crowd and do not face me, or it will be worse for you. Even a fool may be wise after the event.”

Euphorbus would not listen, and said, “Now indeed, Menelaus, shall you pay for the death of my brother, over whom you boasted—whose wife you widowed in her bridal chamber, while you brought unspeakable grief upon his parents. I shall comfort these poor people if I bring your head and armor and place them in the hands of Panthous and noble Phrontis. The time has come for this matter to be fought out and settled, for me or against me.”

As he spoke he struck Menelaus full on the shield, but the spear did not go through, for the shield turned the point. Menelaus then took aim, praying to Father Zeus as he did so. Euphorbus was drawing back, and Menelaus struck him about the roots of his throat, leaning his whole weight on the spear to drive it home. The point went clean through his neck, and his armor rang rattling around him as he fell heavily to the ground. His hair, which was like that of the Graces, and his locks so deftly bound in bands of silver and gold, were all bedrabbled with blood. As when a man has raised a fine young olive tree in a clear space where there is abundance of water—the plant is full of promise, and though the winds beat on it from every quarter it puts forth its white blossoms, until the blasts of some fierce hurricane sweep down upon it and level it with the ground—even so did Menelaus strip the fair youth Euphorbus of his armor after he had slain him. Or as some fierce lion upon the mountains, in the pride of his strength, fastens on the finest heifer in a herd as it is feeding—first he breaks her neck with his strong jaws, and then gorges on her blood and entrails; dogs and shepherds raise a hue and cry against him, but they stand aloof and will not come close, for they are pale with fear—just so, no one had the courage to face valiant Menelaus. The son of Atreus would then have easily carried off the armor of the son of Panthous, had not Phoebus Apollo been angry and, in the guise of Mentes, chief of the Cicones, urged Hector to attack him. “Hector,” he said, “you are now going after the horses of the noble son of Aeacus, but you will not take them; they cannot be kept in hand and driven by mortal man, save only by Achilles, who is the son of an immortal mother. Meanwhile Menelaus, son of Atreus, has stood astride the body of Patroclus and has killed the noblest of the Trojans, Euphorbus, son of Panthous, so that he can fight no more.”

The god then went back into the toil and turmoil, but the soul of Hector was darkened with a cloud of grief. He looked along the ranks and saw Euphorbus lying on the ground, with the blood still flowing from his wound, and Menelaus stripping him of his armor. At this he made his way to the front like a flame of fire, clad in his gleaming armor and crying with a loud voice. When the son of Atreus heard him, he said to himself in his dismay, “Alas, what shall I do? I may not let the Trojans take the armor of Patroclus, who has fallen fighting on my behalf, lest some Danaan who sees me cry shame on me. Still, if for my honor's sake I fight Hector and the Trojans single-handed, they will prove too many for me, for Hector is bringing them up in force. Why, however, should I hesitate? When a man fights against heaven with one whom a god befriends, he will soon rue it. Let no Danaan think ill of me if I give place to Hector, for the hand of heaven is with him. Yet if I could find Ajax, the two of us would fight Hector and heaven too, if only we might save the body of Patroclus for Achilles, son of Peleus. This, of many evils, would be the least.”

While he was thus of two minds, the Trojans came up to him with Hector at their head. So he drew back and left the body, turning about like some bearded lion who is being chased by dogs and men from a stockyard with spears and shouts, whereon he is daunted and slinks sulkily off—just so did Menelaus, son of Atreus, turn and leave the body of Patroclus. When he was among his own men, he looked around for mighty Ajax, son of Telamon, and presently saw him on the extreme left of the fight, cheering on his men and urging them to keep on fighting, for Phoebus Apollo had spread a great panic among them. He ran up to him and said, “Ajax, my good friend, come with me at once to dead Patroclus, if so be that we may take the body to Achilles—as for his armor, Hector already has it.”

These words stirred the heart of Ajax, and he made his way among the front ranks, Menelaus going with him. Hector had stripped Patroclus of his armor and was dragging him away to cut off his head and fling the body before the dogs of Troy. But Ajax came up with his shield like a wall before him, at which Hector withdrew under shelter of his men, and sprang onto his chariot, giving the armor over to the Trojans to take to the city as a great trophy for himself. Ajax, therefore, covered the body of Patroclus with his broad shield and stood astride him, as a lion stands over his whelps if hunters have come upon him in a forest when he is with his little ones—in the pride and fierceness of his strength he draws his knit brows down until they cover his eyes—just so did Ajax stand astride the body of Patroclus, and by his side stood Menelaus, son of Atreus, nursing great sorrow in his heart.

Then Glaucus, son of Hippolochus, looked fiercely at Hector and rebuked him sternly. “Hector,” he said, “you make a brave show, but in fight you are sadly lacking. A runaway like yourself has no claim to so great a reputation. Think how you can now save your town and citadel by the hands of your own people born in Ilium, for you will get no Lycians to fight for you, seeing what thanks they have had for their incessant hardships. Are you likely, sir, to do anything to help a man of less note, after leaving Sarpedon—who was at once your guest and your comrade in arms—to be the spoil and prey of the Danaans? As long as he lived he did good service both to your city and yourself; yet you had no stomach to save his body from the dogs. If the Lycians will listen to me, they will go home and leave Troy to its fate. If the Trojans had any of that daring, fearless spirit that takes hold of men fighting for their country and harassing those who would attack it, we should soon carry off Patroclus into Ilium. Could we get this dead man away and bring him into the city of Priam, the Argives would readily give up the armor of Sarpedon, and we should get his body as well. For he whose squire has now been killed is the foremost man at the ships of the Achaeans—he and his close-fighting followers. Nevertheless, you dared not make a stand against Ajax, nor face him eye-to-eye with battle all round you, for he is a braver man than you are.”

Hector scowled at him and answered, “Glaucus, you should know better. I have held you, until now, as a man of more understanding than any in all Lycia; but now I despise you for saying I am afraid of Ajax. I fear neither battle nor the din of chariots, but Zeus's will is stronger than ours; Zeus at one time makes even a strong man draw back and snatches victory from his grasp, while at another he sets him on to fight. Come here, then, my friend, stand by me, and see whether I shall indeed play the coward the whole day through, as you say, or whether I shall not stay some even of the boldest Danaans from fighting around the body of Patroclus.”

As he spoke, he called loudly to the Trojans, “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians, fighters in close combat, be men, my friends, and fight with might and main, while I put on the fine armor of Achilles, which I took when I killed Patroclus.”

With this, Hector left the fight and ran at full speed after his men, who were taking the armor of Achilles to Troy but had not yet gone far. Standing for a while apart from the woeful fight, he changed his armor. His own he sent to the strong city of Ilium and to the Trojans, while he put on the immortal armor of the son of Peleus, which the gods had given to Peleus, who in his old age gave it to his son. But the son did not grow old in his father's armor.

When Zeus, lord of the storm-cloud, saw Hector standing aloof and arming himself in the armor of the son of Peleus, he shook his head and muttered to himself, saying, “Ah, poor wretch, you arm yourself in the armor of a hero before whom many another trembles, and you care nothing for the doom that is already close upon you. You have killed his comrade, so brave and strong; but it was not right of you to strip the armor from his head and shoulders. I do indeed grant you great might now, but in exchange for this you shall not return from battle to lay the armor of the son of Peleus before Andromache.”

The son of Cronos bowed his portentous brows, and Hector fitted the armor to his body. Terrible Ares entered into him, and filled his whole body with might and valor. With a shout he strode in among the allies, and his armor flashed about him so that he seemed to all of them like the great son of Peleus himself. He went about among them and cheered them on—Mesthles, Glaucus, Medon, Thersilochus, Asteropaeus, Deisenor and Hippothous, Phorcys, Chromius, and Ennomus the augur. All these he urged on, saying, “Hear me, allies from other cities who are here in your thousands. It was not to have a crowd about me that I called you here each from his several city, but that with heart and soul you might defend the wives and little ones of the Trojans from the fierce Achaeans. For this I oppress my people with your food and the presents that make you rich. So turn, and charge at the enemy, to stand or fall as is the way of war. Whoever shall bring Patroclus, dead though he be, into the hands of the Trojans, and shall make Ajax give way before him, I will give him one half the spoils and keep the other. He will thus share equal honor with myself.”

When he had thus spoken, they charged full weight upon the Danaans with their spears held out before them, and every man's hopes ran high that he would force Ajax, son of Telamon, to yield up the body—fools that they were, for he was about to take the lives of many. Then Ajax said to Menelaus, “My good friend Menelaus, you and I shall hardly come out of this fight alive. I am less concerned for the body of Patroclus—who will shortly become meat for the dogs and vultures of Troy—than for the safety of my own head and yours. Hector has wrapped us in a storm of battle from every quarter, and our destruction seems now certain. Call, then, upon the princes of the Danaans, if any can hear us.”

Menelaus did as he said, and shouted to the Danaans for help at the top of his voice. “My friends,” he cried, “princes and counselors of the Argives—all you who drink at the public cost with Agamemnon and Menelaus, and give orders each to his own people as Zeus grants him power and glory—the fight is so thick about me that I cannot distinguish you one from another. Come, then, every man unbidden, and think it shame that Patroclus should become meat and morsel for Trojan hounds.”

Swift Ajax, son of Oileus, heard him and was first to force his way through the fight and run to help him. Next came Idomeneus, and Meriones, his squire, peer of murderous Ares. As for the others that came into the fight after these, who on his own could name them?

The Trojans with Hector at their head charged in a body. As a great wave that comes thundering in at the mouth of some heaven-born river, and the rocks that jut into the sea ring with the roar of the breakers that beat and buffet them—just so did the Trojans come on. But the Achaeans, in singleness of heart, stood firm about the son of Menoetius, and fenced him with their bronze shields. Zeus, moreover, hid the brightness of their helmets in a thick cloud, for he had borne no grudge against the son of Menoetius while he was still alive and squire to the descendant of Aeacus; so he was loath to let him fall a prey to the dogs of his foes the Trojans, and urged his comrades on to defend him.

At first the Trojans drove the Achaeans back, and they withdrew from the dead man daunted. The Trojans did not succeed in killing anyone, but nevertheless they drew the body away. The Achaeans did not lose it long, for Ajax, foremost of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus in stature and prowess, quickly rallied them and made for the front like a wild boar upon the mountains who stands at bay in the forest glades and routs the hounds and lusty youths who have attacked him—just so did Ajax, son of Telamon, passing easily in among the phalanxes of the Trojans, scatter those who had stood astride Patroclus and were most bent on winning glory by dragging him off to their city. At this moment Hippothous, brave son of the Pelasgian Lethus, in his zeal for Hector and the Trojans, was dragging the body off by the foot through the press of the fight, having bound a strap round the sinews near the ankle; but a mischief soon befell him from which none who would gladly have helped could save him, for the son of Telamon sprang forward and struck him on his bronze-cheeked helmet. The plumed headpiece broke about the point of the weapon, struck at once by the spear and by the strong hand of Ajax, so that the bloody brain came oozing out through the crest-socket. His strength failed him and he let Patroclus's foot drop from his hand, as he fell full-length dead upon the body. Thus he died far from the fertile land of Larissa, and never repaid his parents the cost of raising him, for his life was cut short early by the spear of mighty Ajax. Hector then took aim at Ajax with a spear, but he saw it coming and just managed to avoid it; the spear passed on and struck Schedius, son of noble Iphitus, captain of the Phoceans, who dwelt in famed Panopeus and ruled over many people. It struck him under the middle of the collar-bone; the bronze point went right through him, coming out at the bottom of his shoulder blade, and his armor rang rattling round him as he fell heavily to the ground. Ajax in turn struck noble Phorcys, son of Phaenops, in the middle of the belly as he was standing astride Hippothous, and broke the plate of his cuirass, whereupon the spear tore out his entrails and he clutched the ground in his palm as he fell to earth. Hector and those in the front rank then gave ground, while the Argives raised a loud cry of triumph, and drew off the bodies of Phorcys and Hippothous, which they presently stripped of their armor.

The Trojans would now have been worsted by the brave Achaeans and driven back to Ilium through their own cowardice, while the Argives—so great was their courage and endurance—would have won a triumph even against the will of Zeus, had not Apollo roused Aeneas in the likeness of Periphas, son of Epytus, an attendant who had grown old in the service of Aeneas's aged father, and was at all times devoted to him. In that likeness, then, Apollo said, “Aeneas, can you not manage, even though heaven be against us, to save high Ilium? I have known men whose numbers, courage, and self-reliance have saved their people in spite of Zeus—whereas in this case he would much rather give victory to us than to the Danaans, if only you would fight instead of being so terribly afraid.”

Aeneas knew Apollo when he looked straight at him, and shouted to Hector, saying, “Hector, and all other Trojans and allies, shame on us if we are beaten by the Achaeans and driven back to Ilium through our own cowardice. A god has just come up to me and told me that Zeus, the supreme disposer, will be with us. Let us make for the Danaans, then, that it may go hard with them before they carry off dead Patroclus to the ships.”

As he spoke he sprang out far in front of the others, who then rallied and again faced the Achaeans. Aeneas speared Leiocritus, son of Arisbas, a valiant follower of Lycomedes, and Lycomedes was moved with pity as he saw him fall; he therefore went close up and speared Apisaon, son of Hippasus, shepherd of his people, in the liver under the midriff, so that he died. He had come from fertile Paeonia and was the best man of them all after Asteropaeus. Asteropaeus flew forward to avenge him and attack the Danaans, but this was no longer possible, since those about Patroclus were well covered by their shields and held their spears in front of them; for Ajax had given strict orders that no man was either to give ground or to stand out before the others, but all were to hold closely together about the body and fight hand-to-hand. Thus did huge Ajax bid them, and the earth ran red with blood as the corpses fell thick on one another—alike on the side of the Trojans and allies and on that of the Danaans; for these latter too fought no bloodless fight, though many fewer of them perished, through the care they took to defend and stand by one another.

Thus did they fight as if it were a flaming fire. It seemed as though it had gone hard even with the sun and moon, for they were hidden over all that part where the bravest heroes were fighting about the dead son of Menoetius, while the other Danaans and Achaeans fought at their ease in full daylight with brilliant sunshine all around them, and there was not a cloud to be seen on plain or mountain. These last, moreover, would rest for a while and leave off fighting, since they were some distance apart and beyond the range of one another's weapons; whereas those in the thick of the fray suffered both from battle and from darkness. All the best of them were being worn out by the great weight of their armor, but the two valiant heroes, Thrasymedes and Antilochus, had not yet heard of the death of Patroclus, and believed him still to be alive and leading the van against the Trojans. They were keeping themselves in reserve against the death or rout of their own comrades, for so Nestor had ordered when he sent them from the ships into battle.

So through the livelong day did they wage fierce war, and the sweat of their toil rained ever on their legs beneath them, and on their hands and eyes, as they fought over the squire of the swift son of Peleus. It was as when a man gives a great ox-hide, all drenched in fat, to his men and bids them stretch it; they stand round it in a ring and tug until the moisture leaves it, and the fat soaks in through the many who pull at it, and it is well stretched—just so did the two sides tug the dead body here and there within the compass of but a little space. The Trojans were steadfastly set on dragging it into Ilium, while the Achaeans were no less so on taking it to their ships; and fierce was the fight between them. Not Ares himself, lord of hosts, nor yet Athena, even in their fullest fury, could have made light of such a battle.

Such fearful turmoil of men and horses did Zeus on that day ordain round the body of Patroclus. Meanwhile Achilles did not know that he had fallen, for the fight was under the wall of Troy, a long way off the ships. He had no idea, therefore, that Patroclus was dead, and thought he would return alive as soon as he had gone close up to the gates. He knew Patroclus was not to sack the city, neither with nor without his help, for his mother had often told him this when he sat alone with her, and she had informed him of the counsels of great Zeus. Now, however, she had not told him how great a disaster had befallen him in the death of the one who was far dearest to him of all his comrades.

The others still kept on charging one another round the body with their pointed spears and killing each other. Then one would say, “My friends, we can never again show our faces at the ships—better, and far better, that earth should open and swallow us here in this place, than that we should let the Trojans have the triumph of carrying off Patroclus to their city.”

The Trojans on their part spoke to one another, saying, “Friends, though we fall to a man beside this body, let none shrink from fighting.” With such words did they urge each other on. They fought and fought, and an iron clangor rose through the empty air to the brazen vault of heaven. The horses of the descendant of Aeacus stood out of the fight and wept when they heard that their driver had been laid low by the hand of murderous Hector. Automedon, valiant son of Diores, lashed them again and again; many a time did he speak kindly to them, and many a time did he rebuke them, but they would neither go back to the ships by the waters of the broad Hellespont, nor yet into battle among the Achaeans. They stood with their chariot stock-still, like a pillar set over the tomb of some dead man or woman, and bowed their heads to the ground. Hot tears fell from their eyes as they mourned the loss of their charioteer, and their noble manes drooped all wet from under the yoke-straps on either side of the yoke.

The son of Cronos saw them and took pity on their sorrow. He shook his head and muttered to himself, “Poor things, why did we give you to King Peleus, who is a mortal, while you are yourselves ageless and immortal? Was it so you might share the sorrows that befall mankind? For of all creatures that live and move upon the earth, there is none so pitiable as he is. Still, Hector, son of Priam, shall drive neither you nor your chariot. I will not have it. It is enough that he should have the armor over which he boasts so vainly. Furthermore, I will give you strength of heart and limb to bear Automedon safely to the ships from the battle, for I shall let the Trojans triumph still further, and go on killing until they reach the ships; whereupon night shall fall and darkness overshadow the land.”

As he spoke he breathed heart and strength into the horses, so that they shook the dust from their manes and bore their chariot swiftly into the fight that raged between Trojans and Achaeans. Behind them fought Automedon, full of sorrow for his comrade, like a vulture amid a flock of geese. In and out, here and there, at full speed he dashed amid the throng of Trojans; but for all the fury of his pursuit he killed no man, for he could not wield his spear and keep his horses in hand when alone in the chariot. At last, however, a comrade, Alcimedon, son of Laerces, son of Haemon, caught sight of him and came up behind his chariot. “Automedon,” he said, “what god has put this folly into your heart and robbed you of your right mind, that you fight the Trojans in the front rank single-handed? He who was your comrade is slain, and Hector plumes himself on being armed in the armor of the descendant of Aeacus.”
